title: [1.28.2] Keeps zfs pool busy on UnmountVolume via csi-provider
body:
### What happened?

We are running our custom csi provider to mount zfs via iscsi, this is operating since at least 1.20 and never showed any issues.

It does not implement the NodeStage / NodeUnstage apis, and only uses the NodePublishVolume / NodeUnpublishVolume.

Since upgrading to 1.28.2 the Unmount progress gets stuck and the zfs pool keeps busy indefinitely.

A solution to fix the stuck pool is to delete the folder of the pv inside of the pod, this leads to log spam by kubelet it can't find the corresponding .json file for the csi provider, and a restart of kubelet afterwards allows the pool to be actually exported.

### What did you expect to happen?

Do not keep the mounted volume busy when Unmounting via CSI providers.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Possibly other providers also see those issues?

### Anything else we need to know?

Kubelet logs the following, whereas the message is passed from the csi plugin:

```
Sep 28 08:18:26 at-host-41 kubelet[3179792]: E0928 08:18:26.861506 3179792 nestedpendingoperations.go:348] Operation for "{volumeName:kubernetes.io/csi/anchor.storage.creamfinance.com^v-758fa692-ad4d-4cc5-8f20-18b8770bcbd5 podName:3741aca2-e297-4d4c-a2ff-3978a62f043e nodeName:}" failed. No retries permitted until 2023-09-28 08:20:28.861466917 +0000 UTC m=+1190473.720166002 (durationBeforeRetry 2m2s). Error: UnmountVolume.TearDown failed for volume "pgdata" (UniqueName: "kubernetes.io/csi/anchor.storage.creamfinance.com^v-758fa692-ad4d-4cc5-8f20-18b8770bcbd5") pod "3741aca2-e297-4d4c-a2ff-3978a62f043e" (UID: "3741aca2-e297-4d4c-a2ff-3978a62f043e") : kubernetes.io/csi: Unmounter.TearDownAt failed: rpc error: code = Internal desc = cannot export 'v-758fa692-ad4d-4cc5-8f20-18b8770bcbd5': pool is busy (exit status 1)
```

When deleting the corresponding directory (/var/lib/kubelet/pods/3741aca2-e297-4d4c-a2ff-3978a62f043e/volumes/kubernetes.io~csi/pv-758fa692-ad4d-4cc5-8f20-18b8770bcbd5) as described, it spams the log with following message:

Deleting the mount directory inside of /var/lib/kubelet/pods/3741aca2-e297-4d4c-a2ff-3978a62f043e/volumes/kubernetes.io~csi/pv-758fa692-ad4d-4cc5-8f20-18b8770bcbd5 releases the "busy" pool and allows to proceed with the unmount.

In the operator I was first exporting the zfs pool and then deleting the mount folder, I have switched those two steps and now it seems to work correctly again.

title: External service UDP fails while TCP works due to definition processing asymmetry
body:
### What happened?

I have a single node k3s installation. I'd like to use it as an entry point even if some services are installed on separate VMs, not on K8s. External services work nicely when the service is available via TCP, but not when it's UDP as the system thinks UDP service doesn't have Endpoint definition and creates deny rules for iptables. The YAML is symmetric to the TCP one.

Working TCP:
````
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: bugreport-works
  namespace: mate
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  ports:
  - port: 4321
    name: works-tcp
    protocol: TCP
    targetPort: 4321
---
kind: Endpoints
apiVersion: v1
metadata:
  name: bugreport-works
  namespace: mate
subsets:
  - addresses:
      - ip: 192.168.122.108
    ports:
      - port: 4321
        name: works-tcp
````

Not working UDP:
````
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: bugreport-fails
  namespace: mate
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  ports:
  - port: 4321
    name: fails-udp
    protocol: UDP
    targetPort: 4321
---
kind: Endpoints
apiVersion: v1
metadata:
  name: bugreport-fails
  namespace: mate
subsets:
  - addresses:
      - ip: 192.168.122.108
    ports:
      - port: 4321
        name: fails-udp
````

For UDP I see these generated rejection rules (for TCP, there is no any similar):
```
-A KUBE-EXTERNAL-SERVICES -d 192.168.31.133/32 -p udp -m comment --comment "mate/bugreport-fails:fails-udp has no endpoints" -m udp --dport 4321 -j REJECT --reject-with icmp-port-unreachable
-A KUBE-EXTERNAL-SERVICES -p udp -m comment --comment "mate/bugreport-fails:fails-udp has no endpoints" -m addrtype --dst-type LOCAL -m udp --dport 31974 -j REJECT --reject-with icmp-port-unreachable
-A KUBE-SERVICES -d 10.43.215.148/32 -p udp -m comment --comment "mate/bugreport-fails:fails-udp has no endpoints" -m udp --dport 4321 -j REJECT --reject-with icmp-port-unreachable
```

### What did you expect to happen?

TCP and UDP definitions should work identically

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Modify the definitions above according to your environment. Get an external host (VM, node, etc), netcat is the easiest to test it.
On caller client (first for TCP, second for UDP)
```
root@hu1l2022978:~# nc 192.168.31.133 4321
a
b
^C
root@hu1l2022978:~# nc-u 192.168.31.133 4321
a
root@hu1l2022978:~#
```
On backend host (first for TCP, second for UDP)
```
root@matelin:~# nc -ul 4321
^C
root@matelin:~# nc -l 4321
a
b
root@matelin:~# nc -ul 4321
```

In case of applying the UDP definition, on K8S node you immediately see the rejection rules (see above)

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

title: When deleting pods on the same node in batches, the exited container may remain, causing pod records to remain.
body:
### What happened?

During performance testing, I found that when deleting pods on a node in batches, such as 100, the problem of pod deletion failure may occur. The exited container may remain, causing pod records to remain. I think this problem is related to the implementation of pod_container_deletor.go that containerDeletorBufferLimit is only 50. and in the func (p *podContainerDeletor) deleteContainersInPod, when the worker channel is full, it discards the event. I think using work queue instead of channel is a better solution. And the processing logic of runtime.DeleteContainer needs to be optimized. The processing can be skipped for containers that have been externally deleted or cannot be found. 

And i found it still almost the same solution in podContainerDeletor. The master branch may also have the same problem.

I will submit a PR later for this issue.



### What did you expect to happen?

pods and containers can be deleted successfully

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

batch delete over than 100 pods that on same node

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

### Kubernetes version

$ kubectl version

nodes.title: Remove an old compatibility check/warning
nodes.body:
What type of PR is this?

/kind cleanup
/sig network
/area ipvs
/area kube-proxy

What this PR does / why we need it:
kube-proxy used to unconditionally load the br-netfilter kernel module and set the bridge-nf-call-iptables sysctl. In https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/20647 this was moved to the kubenet plugin instead (since it is not needed and not wanted for some other network plugins), and kube-proxy was changed to just warn if br-netfilter was not loaded / bridge-nf-call-iptables was not set, with the comment "Until most plugins handle this, log when config is missing". That was seven and a half years ago. Presumably everyone got the message by now.

(Note also that the check and the warning are both IPv4-specific; to make kube-proxy work correctly with linux-bridge-based plugins under IPv6, you need to set bridge-nf-call-ip6tables instead. e.g., this was fixed in kubeadm in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/53013, but no one ever suggested that maybe kube-proxy should warn people about that...)

Which issue(s) this PR fixes:
Fixes #120849 

 Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```NONE```

title: How to setup a warmup period for the scaled-out replicas in Kubernetes?
body:
### What happened?

We are using Istio version 1.18.2 on all our AKS (V1.27.3) based envts (Dev,Stg, Prod, Dr, etc.) setup. We have enabled the Istio sidecars injection with namespace injection for Springboot java-based applications.

During our scalability tests, we noticed that when a service scales out, (i.e. from 3 to 4 instances), the new instance after reporting being healthy immediately gets i.e. 25% of the load. Since the service instance did not have a chance to warm up yet, requests sent to it temporarily time out or show increased response time compared to other existing instances. This state can remain from 3-4 minutes to even 15 minutes, depending on the load, from what we saw in our tastings.



### What did you expect to happen?

We were looking for a scaling related solution so that a new service instances right after scaling out to receive load that they are able to handle.
so that scaling out does not cause temporary response time to increase for the production services. 


We searched for a solution from istio side and tried as per the solution provided here for Destination Rule. 
https://stackoverflow.com/questions/74517652/gradually-warm-java-application-in-k8s-with-istio#:~:text=trafficPolicy%3A%0A%20%20%20%20loadBalancer%3A%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20simple%3A%20ROUND_ROBIN%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20warmupDurationSecs%3A%20180s 

    apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1alpha3
    kind: DestinationRule
    metadata:
      name: myapp
      namespace: myns
    spec:
      host: "myapp.myns.svc.cluster.local"
      trafficPolicy:
        loadBalancer:
          simple: ROUND_ROBIN
          warmupDurationSecs: "180s"
      subsets:
        - name: v1
          labels:
            app: myapp
            version: 1.0

In our destination rule, we haven't configured different versions for subsets, and it will be always v1.0 (we don't require the different versions as of now). But this solution of traffic policy also didn't worked as expected, as we tested the scaling behavior and not anew release.

is there any way to achieve this using istio while scaleout happening. ?

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

when a service scales out, (i.e. from 3 to 4 instances), the new instance after reporting being healthy immediately gets i.e. 25% of the load. Since the service instance did not have a chance to warm up yet, requests sent to it temporarily time out or show increased response time compared to other existing instances. This state can remain from 3-4 minutes to even 15 minutes, depending on the load, from what we saw in our tastings.

title: Which cert does kubelet used actually?
body:
### What happened?

Our cluster recently encountered issues with certificate renewal, a master node  failed to renew certificate from apiserver  becuase there is out-dated base64 encoded kubelet.conf I think that's why kubelet cannot renew `kubelet-client-current.pem`.


### What did you expect to happen?

cert in kubelet.conf should point to `/var/lib/kublet/pki/kubelet-client-current.pem` after TLS bootstrap after finished cluster initialization instead of a base64 encoded cert.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

No need to reproduce.

### Anything else we need to know?

According to the [doc](https://kubernetes.io/docs/setup/production-environment/tools/kubeadm/kubelet-integration/#workflow-when-using-kubeadm-join), base64 encoded cert should only used in kubelet start phase, but what if both cert provided in kubelet.conf and `/var/lib/kubelet/pki/kubelet-client-current.pem`, which cert does kubelet used for communicate with apiserver acutally ? 
Also the [warning](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/kubeadm/kubeadm-certs/#:~:text=rotation%20fails.-,Warning,-%3A) says base64 encoed cert only appears prior to 1.17 which makes confused because our cluster is 1.18

> which cert does kubelet used for communicate with apiserver actually ?

i think the kubelet prefers the current certificate file over the base64 encoded certificate, as stated in [this document](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/tls/certificate-rotation/).

> > which cert does kubelet used for communicate with apiserver actually ?
> 
> i think the kubelet prefers the current certificate file over the base64 encoded certificate, as stated in [this document](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/tls/certificate-rotation/).

Thanks for response. I think kubelet use the base64 encoded cert in kubelet.conf acquire a new certificate from apiserver and using `kubelet-client-current.pem` to communicate with apisever,right ? 
Another question confuses me is that doc says since 1.18 cert in kubelet.conf should point to cert in `/var/lib/kubelet/pki/kubelet-client-current.pem`, but why is this an exception?

@stricklandye You are welcome! 
Yes, you are correct. The `kubelet` uses the base64 encoded certificate in **kubelet.conf** to acquire a new certificate from the `apiserver`, and then uses the **kubelet-client-current.pem** file to communicate with the `apiserver`. This is how the `kubelet` performs **TLS bootstrapping**, which is a process of requesting a signed certificate from the apiserver and storing it in a local file for future use. The **kubelet.conf** file is updated with the path to the local file, so that the `kubelet` can use it for subsequent connections.

you can refer to these resources to understand this better :

- [TLS Bootstrapping | Kubernetes](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/kubelet-tls-bootstrapping/): This is a document that explains how the kubelet performs TLS bootstrapping, which is the process of requesting a signed certificate from the apiserver and storing it in a local file for future use.
- [Issue #581](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubeadm/issues/581): This is an issue on GitHub that discusses the problem of certificate renewal in Kubernetes clusters created with kubeadm, and some possible solutions to fix it.

> Another question confuses me is that doc says since 1.18 cert in kubelet.conf should point to cert in /var/lib/kubelet/pki/kubelet-client-current.pem, but why is this an exception?

This is a good question. The documentation says that since 1.18, the cert in **kubelet.conf** should point to the cert in **/var/lib/kubelet/pki/kubelet-client-current.pem**, which is the file that contains the rotated kubelet client certificate. However, this is not always the case, as there are some exceptions:

- One exception is when you use `kubeadm` to create a cluster with an external CA (certificate authority). In this case, `kubeadm` will not generate a **kubelet.conf** file for you, and you have to create it manually. You also have to provide the base64 encoded certificate and key in the **kubelet.conf** file. you can refer to [this](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/64850658/how-to-add-certificates-to-kube-config-file) and [this](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/kubeadm/kubeadm-certs/#:~:text=External%20CA%20mode&text=If%20all%20other%20certificates%20and,the%20CA%20certificate%20and%20key.).

- Another exception is when you use `kubeadm` to upgrade a cluster from a version prior to 1.17 to a version 1.18 or later. In this case, `kubeadm` will not update the **kubelet.conf** file for you, and you have to modify it manually to point to the rotated certificate file, as explained  [here](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/kubeadm/kubeadm-certs/).

These exceptions are due to some limitations of `kubeadm` and the way it handles **certificate management**. 
I hope this answers your question.

1.18 was dropped from support a long time ago.
i recall a kubeadm bug where the node where "kubeadm init" was called got the embedded cert/key in kubelet.conf instead of the links to files.

this was fixed a long time ago in kubeadm.
please fix it manually in your cluster by editing the kubelet.conf and then restarting the kubelet.
and try to upgrade to >=1.25.

title: Volumes are forcibly detached when CSI driver installation is broken and KCM switches leader
body:
### What happened?

On an EKS cluster, we observed that volumes are forcibly detached after 6mins (`maxWaitForUnmountDuration`) after KCM leader switches. The EBS CSI Driver is missing at that time. Related logs:
```
14:51:22Z 11 attach_detach_controller.go:440] Error creating spec for volume "pv", pod "sdb"/"scout-14": error performing CSI migration checks and translation for PVC "sdb"/"pv-scout-14": in-tree plugin kubernetes.io/aws-ebs is migrated on node xxx but driver ebs.csi.aws.com is not installed
...
14:57:23Z 11 reconciler.go:227] attacherDetacher.DetachVolume started for volume "nil" (UniqueName: "kubernetes.io/csi/ebs.csi.aws.com^vol-06b79540fd7b6c2cb") on node "xxx" This volume is not safe to detach, but maxWaitForUnmountDuration 6m0s expired, force detaching
```

The EBS CSI Driver was removed from nodes after the volumes were attached to pods. The volumes remained attached until KCM switched leader. When new KCM acquired lease, it restarted the Attach/Detach controller. Due to missing CSI Driver, function `CreateVolumeSpec` failed in `populateDesiredStateOfWorld` (which would only run on the start of A/D controller) - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.23.17/pkg/controller/volume/attachdetach/attach_detach_controller.go#L440-L446. As a result, `volumeSpec` remained nil. And the volumes were treated as if they were not used by any pods and were forcibly detached after maxWaitForUnmountDuration.

I found the failure mode in CSI migration KEP https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/master/keps/sig-storage/625-csi-migration/README.md#troubleshooting, that:

> If the CSI driver is missing but the PVC already exists. Volume attach/detach will fail with the following log in Kube-Controller-Manager:
```
E0125 11:54:12.388111       9 util.go:239] Error processing volume "mypvc" for pod "default"/"web-server": error performing CSI migration checks and translation for PVC "default"/"podpvc-intree": in-tree plugin kubernetes.io/gce-pd is migrated on node kubernetes-minion-group-hsv0 but driver pd.csi.storage.gke.io is not installed
```
So ideally volumes should not be attached/detached when CSI driver is missing, while we observed volumes were detached forcibly by KCM when leader switch occurred, while CSI driver was missing.

### What did you expect to happen?

Volume should not be detached when CSI driver is missing regardless of KCM leader switching.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

- Install CSI Driver on some worker nodes of a kubernetes cluster
- Create some pods on these worker nodes and attach volumes to pods
- Break or remove the CSI Driver installation on these nodes
- Let KCM switch leader
- Observe volumes detach event in KCM log

### Anything else we need to know?

The issue was observed on 1.23.17 version cluster, but looks into latest code seems the logic stays the same so suspect the same issue would occur on 1.27 cluster as well.

### Kubernetes version

1.23.17



### Cloud provider

<details>
AWS
</details>

$ cat /etc/os-release
# paste output here
$ uname -a
# paste output here

C:\> wmic os get Caption, Version, BuildNumber, OSArchitecture

title: Updating pods during scheduling may produce dirty data
body:
### What happened?

If we update a pod（such as update annotation） during the scheduling process, the scheduler's podInformer will generate an update event. If the pod has not been assumed at this time, this event will be added to the scheduling queue. When the pod is scheduled succeed, since the pod is still in the scheduling queue, the pod may be scheduled again. 

If there are many pods in the scheduling queue, the pod cannot be scheduled until 30 seconds later. At this time, the pod information in assumedPods has been cleared, and the pod will be scheduled again. Since the pod has been scheduled succeed, this scheduling will fail, and the scheduler will continue to retry, repeating the cycle. This pod will always become dirty data in the scheduler unless the scheduler is restarted.


### What did you expect to happen?

If the pod has been scheduled succeed, the scheduler should not schedule dirty data in the queue.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a pod；
2. When the pod starts scheduling, update the pod before assume（This step can be achieved by adding breakpoints through local debugging）；
3. After the update event generated by the pod enters the scheduling queue, we should guaranteed the pod  to be scheduled again after 30 seconds（Implemented through local breakpoint debugging）；
4. The pod has been scheduled, but the scheduler is still scheduling the pod in a loop.

### Anything else we need to know?

title: Kubelet log query errors "input contains unsupported characters"
body:
### What happened?

I enabled the [kubelet log query feature](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/cluster-administration/system-logs/#log-query) on EKS 1.27.4 using Ubuntu 20.04.6.

When I try to query the kubelet logs or log files from the system I get the error "input contains unsupported characters"

```
kubectl get --raw "/api/v1/nodes/i-0ede67f2d75dfe308.us-west-2.compute.internal/proxy/logs/?query=snap.kubelet-eks.daemon.service"
Error from server (NotAcceptable): query: Invalid value: "snap.kubelet-eks.daemon.service": input contains unsupported characters

kubectl get --raw "/api/v1/nodes/i-0ede67f2d75dfe308.us-west-2.compute.internal/proxy/logs/?query=cloud-init.log"
Error from server (NotAcceptable): query: Invalid value: "cloud-init.log": input contains unsupported characters
```
The systemd kubelet service runs as a snap called `snap.kubelet-eks.daemon.service` and I _think_ that might be the source of this problem (running the kubelet in a snap), but I'm not sure if it's intended to work. The fact that I couldn't see /var/log file query was surprising and the error message is misleading which is why I'm opening an issue here.

I followed the same configuration steps on Amazon Linux 2 and it works as expected.


### What did you expect to happen?

Log query should work on Ubuntu or provide a clearer error message.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

This should be reproducible on any Kubernetes cluster running Ubuntu with Kubelet in a snap, but this is what I did.

Install [eksdemo](https://github.com/awslabs/eksdemo) to make cluster creation and karpenter setup easier)
```
eksdemo create cluster log-testing --os Ubuntu2004 --prefix-assignment
```
Install Karpenter as a node autoscaler. This will automatically create a provisioner and AWSNodeTemplate objects.
```
eksdemo install autoscaling karpenter -c ubuntu -A Ubuntu
```
Modify the AWSNodeTemplate with userdata that can customize Ubuntu with log query enabled
```
cat << EOF | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: karpenter.k8s.aws/v1alpha1
kind: AWSNodeTemplate
metadata:
  name: default
spec:
  amiFamily: Ubuntu
  securityGroupSelector:
    aws:eks:cluster-name: ubuntu
  subnetSelector:
    Name: eksctl-ubuntu-cluster/SubnetPrivate*
  userData: |
    #!/bin/bash
    set -e

    # This probably isn't the best way to do this but it worked
    sed -i 's/args="$KUBELET_EXTRA_ARGS"/args="--feature-gates=NodeLogQuery=true $KUBELET_EXTRA_ARGS"/g' /etc/eks/bootstrap.sh
    sed -i '/# writes kubeReserved and evictionHard/a echo "$(jq .enableSystemLogHandler=true $KUBELET_CONFIG)" > $KUBELET_CONFIG' /etc/eks/bootstrap.sh
    sed -i '/# writes kubeReserved and evictionHard/a echo "$(jq .enableSystemLogQuery=true $KUBELET_CONFIG)" > $KUBELET_CONFIG' /etc/eks/bootstrap.sh
EOF
```
Deploy a workload that uses hostname spread to get more nodes.
```
cat << EOF | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: myapp
spec:
  minAvailable: "80%"
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: myapp
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: myapp
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: myapp
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: myapp
    spec:
      containers:
      - image: public.ecr.aws/eks-distro/kubernetes/pause:3.2
        name: myapp
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "1"
            memory: 256M
      topologySpreadConstraints:
      - labelSelector:
          matchLabels:
            app: host-zone-spread
        maxSkew: 2
        topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
        whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
      - labelSelector:
          matchLabels:
            app: host-zone-spread
        maxSkew: 5
        topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
        whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
EOF
```
When the new Ubuntu node is created you can log into the node with session manager. I like to use [ssm-helpers](https://github.com/disneystreaming/ssm-helpers)
```
brew install disneystreaming/tap/ssm-helpers
ssm session
# select the new node
```
You can verify that the kubelet is running and logging is enabled
```
sudo systemctl status -l snap.kubelet-eks.daemon.service
```
Now you can try to query logs
```
kubectl get --raw "/api/v1/nodes/$NODE/proxy/logs/?query=snap.kubelet-eks.daemon.service"
```


### Anything else we need to know?

This works with AL2. You can test with a different AWSNodeTemplate that uses AL2 instead
```
cat << EOF | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: karpenter.k8s.aws/v1alpha1
kind: AWSNodeTemplate
metadata:
  name: default
spec:
  amiFamily: AL2
  securityGroupSelector:
    aws:eks:cluster-name: ubuntu
  subnetSelector:
    Name: eksctl-ubuntu-cluster/SubnetPrivate*
  userData: |
    #!/bin/bash
    set -e

    cat << EOF > /etc/systemd/system/kubelet.service.d/90-kubelet-extra-args.conf
    [Service]
    Environment="KUBELET_EXTRA_ARGS=--feature-gates=NodeLogQuery=true $KUBELET_EXTRA_ARGS"
    EOF
    systemctl daemon-reload

    echo "$(jq '.enableSystemLogHandler=true' /etc/kubernetes/kubelet/kubelet-config.json)" > /etc/kubernetes/kubelet/kubelet-config.json
    echo "$(jq '.enableSystemLogQuery=true' /etc/kubernetes/kubelet/kubelet-config.json)" > /etc/kubernetes/kubelet/kubelet-config.json
EOF
```

title: kube-proxy discards command line args
body:
### What happened?

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/55261 introduced a change to reload config from file and this happens after parsing all the command line flags and hence discards all the command line flags. 

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/35199e42a41f83520e640fbfa9f409516faa7501/cmd/kube-proxy/app/server.go#L245-L259

### What did you expect to happen?

kube-proxy should respect all the command line arguments and if for some reason we need to load config from file we must do it in a way that preserves all command line flags. 

I'm trying to add three additional configuration params to kube-proxy in  https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/120354
1. **conntrack-tcp-be-liberal**
2. **conntrack-udp-timeout**
3. **conntrack-udp-timeout-stream**

I'm not able to use 2 and 3 via command line args. 1 works as I'm syncing it manually.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

If I comment out the following line and rebuild kube-proxy for the local kind cluster, kube-proxy fails with the following logs:

```
I0912 12:58:03.614728       1 server_others.go:367] "GetConntrackMax: using scaled conntrack-max-per-core"
I0912 12:58:03.614756       1 conntrack.go:118] "Set sysctl" entry="net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_max" value=655360
E0912 12:58:03.614765       1 server.go:557] "Error running ProxyServer" err="open /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_max: permission denied"
E0912 12:58:03.614775       1 run.go:74] "command failed" err="open /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_max: permission denied"
```
I guess after commenting out the following line kube-proxy actually tries to run conntrack sysctls and since kind /proc/sys is read-only for kind it fails.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/35199e42a41f83520e640fbfa9f409516faa7501/cmd/kube-proxy/app/server.go#L259


### Anything else we need to know?

Current Flow:

```go
// 1. initialize options
// this internally calls newKubeProxyConfiguration() which generates kube-proxy config with default values
opts := NewOptions()

// 2. add command-line flags
opts.AddFlags(fs)

// 3. complete all the required flags, read config from the file losing defaults and
// values provided by command line flags
opts.Complete()

// 4. validate all the required options
opts.Validate()

// 5. run the kube-proxy
opts.Run()
```

In step 3 we lose all the default and pflag values.

Kustomize Version: v5.0.4-0.20230601165947-6ce0bf390ce3

title: service nodeport cannot be released promptly.
body:
### What happened?

Why PatchService method is used for deleting finalizers in cloud-controller-manager,
[https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/cloud-provider/controllers/service/controller.go#L922 ](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/cloud-provider/controllers/service/controller.go#L922 )
```golang
// removeFinalizer patches the service to remove finalizer.
func (c *Controller) removeFinalizer(service *v1.Service) error {
	if !servicehelper.HasLBFinalizer(service) {
		return nil
	}
	// Make a copy so we don't mutate the shared informer cache.
	updated := service.DeepCopy()
	updated.ObjectMeta.Finalizers = removeString(updated.ObjectMeta.Finalizers, servicehelper.LoadBalancerCleanupFinalizer)

	klog.V(2).Infof("Removing finalizer from service %s/%s", updated.Namespace, updated.Name)
	_, err := servicehelper.PatchService(c.kubeClient.CoreV1(), service, updated)
	return err
}
``` 
This method updates with service/status,
```golang
// PatchService patches the given service's Status or ObjectMeta based on the original and
// updated ones. Change to spec will be ignored.
func PatchService(c corev1.CoreV1Interface, oldSvc, newSvc *v1.Service) (*v1.Service, error) {
	// Reset spec to make sure only patch for Status or ObjectMeta.
	newSvc.Spec = oldSvc.Spec

	patchBytes, err := getPatchBytes(oldSvc, newSvc)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}

	return c.Services(oldSvc.Namespace).Patch(context.TODO(), oldSvc.Name, types.StrategicMergePatchType, patchBytes, metav1.PatchOptions{}, "status")

}
```
[https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/cloud-provider/service/helpers/helper.go#L132](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/cloud-provider/service/helpers/helper.go#L132)
It seems to go unnoticed by the API server, resulting in the API server being unaware when the finalizer field on the service is deleted, leading to a delay in the release of service-related NodePorts.

### What did you expect to happen?

service nodeport be released promptly when service is deleted.

nodes.title: sync Service API status rest storage
nodes.body:
The Service API Rest implementation is complex and has to use different hooks on the REST storage. The status store was making a shallow copy of the storage before adding the hooks, so it was not inheriting the hooks.

The status store must have the same hooks as the rest store to be able to handle correctly the allocation and deallocation of ClusterIPs and nodePorts.


/kind bug
Fixes #120536


```release-note
Fixes a bug where Services using finalizers may hold onto ClusterIP and/or NodePort allocated resources for longer than expected if the finalizer is removed using the status subresource
```

title: Cloud provider implementations do not show provider-specific options in usage string
body:
### What happened?

The `NewCloudControllerManagerCommand` function in `k8s.io/cloud-provider/app/controllermanager.go` accepts an `additionalFlags` parameter which it describes as a way to "controller specific flags to be included in the complete set of controller manager flags". However, when the usage string is shown (either via `$cmd --help` or when parsing options fails), these additional options are not included in the usage string.	

This was identified via code inspection while trying to figure out what options did in `openstack-cloud-controller-manager`.

### What did you expect to happen?

For e.g. `aws-cloud-controller-manager`, the output of `aws-cloud-controller-manager --help` should include a `Tagging Controller Options` section corresponding to [the flagset registered for that command](https://github.com/kubernetes/cloud-provider-aws/blob/v1.28.1/cmd/aws-cloud-controller-manager/main.go#L67-L83). This section should in turn list all of [the options added to that flagset](https://github.com/kubernetes/cloud-provider-aws/blob/v1.28.1/pkg/controllers/options/tagging_controller.go#L30-L38).

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Build a cloud provider executable that includes additional options, such as `aws-cloud-controller-manager`
2. Run `$cmd --help`
3. Observe the additional options are not shown in the output

title: kube-apiserver instability for k8s 1.27.5
body:
### What happened?

Since upgrading to Kubernetes `1.27.5` (from 1.27.4) we have experienced outages on our `kube-apiserver` pods where their container has been restarted due to failing liveness probes.

This has caused instability, usually via a number of important components within our clusters failing leader elections due to timeouts.
There haven't been many outages, but enough to be annoying. Prior to the upgrade the cluster was pretty rock solid.

### What did you expect to happen?

Not having the kube-apiserver fail its liveness probes and have its container restarted.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

I'm not sure. The problem is infrequent and no unusual activity seems to be happening on the cluster that I can detect.
For us we upgraded from version 1.27.4 to 1.27.5 of k8s.

### Anything else we need to know?

We have values set for the number of in-flight requests for the API server set, as well as the `EventRateLimit` adminission controller enabled and configured like so:

kind: Configuration
limits:
- burst: 500
  qps: 250
  type: Namespace
- burst: 250
  qps: 50
  type: User
```

These settings have been in place for our cluster for many months now across a number of k8s versions and haven't posed any problems, but mentioned them in case they are relevant.

The control-plane nodes had plenty of free resources at the time of the problems as well, using roughly 20% of their CPU, and under half their RAM (< 4GiB used on systems with 8GiB available).

@yt2985, can you take a look?

Hi @rxwang662001, may I know how did you generate the service account , secret and the pod? Does the secret has the servicaccount annotation? And has the secret is mounted with the pod? Did you change any default flag value when you enable the cleaner? I am trying to elucidate what happened. It's strange that if the secret is not the autogenerated token, it should not be cleaned. If you can provide more information for me to debug, that would be helpful! Thank you very much!

The autogenerated serviceaccount token needs to mount to the pod before it can be used by the pod, like shown in the link line: https://github.com/yt2985/kubernetes/blob/595a57940a45f25bad4621548ee990c81779c12e/pkg/controller/serviceaccount/legacy_serviceaccount_token_cleaner_test.go#L106 I guess you just add the service account annotation to the pod, but not mount the secret itself. Besides this, I am also curious the legacy-service-account-token-clean-up-period value you used to enable the cleaner. It looks the secret was deleted at the same day as it was created.

@yt2985 
May you check the first bug I reported in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/120298 which wasn't answered, this one is a follow-up to report new issue.

1) I generated a long-live token for the service account referring to https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-service-account/#manually-create-a-long-lived-api-token-for-a-serviceaccount
, then it has same  "type: kubernetes.io/service-account-token" as autogenerated  secret, that's why it could be cleaned I think.

2) with same method I created two serviceaccount, one is referred to in pod, one isn't, but both of them were cleaned, that's why I reported this bug. 
Yes, I didn't mount the secret into the pod, I got your point, shall try too.

3) no, the clean happened just 1 day after, that's why I asked in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/120298 
"since DefaultCleanerSyncInterval = 24 * time.Hour, the cleaner works every 24 hours?"

Hi @rxwang662001，I replied in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/120298, there may be something wrong with the cleaner policy, I will check that. For the third point, the cleaner works every 24 hours and we don't have a way to change it. And I saw you set `--legacy-service-account-token-clean-up-period=1h` when you enabled the cleaner, so once the cleaner works, the token will be deleted. This is the expected behavior. If you don't change the `--legacy-service-account-token-clean-up-period`, the default value is one year. In beta, we will not delete the token directly, instead, we will make it invalid first. You may refer the KEP doc here: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-auth/2799-reduction-of-secret-based-service-account-token#legacyserviceaccounttokencleanup

> I generated a long-live token for the service account referring to https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-service-account/#manually-create-a-long-lived-api-token-for-a-serviceaccount
, then it has same "type: kubernetes.io/service-account-token" as autogenerated secret, that's why it could be cleaned I think.

The manually created token is different from the autogenerated token, though both of them are the "type: kubernetes.io/service-account-token". The autogenerated secret name will be added to the service account, but the manually created will not. Have you added the secret name to the service account? If not, the secret should not be deleted.

> with same method I created two serviceaccount, one is referred to in pod, one isn't, but both of them were cleaned, that's why I reported this bug.

How did you create the serviceaccounts? The serviceaccounts should not be cleaned by the cleaner.

After mounting the secret with long-live token into the pod manually it works as expected that secret won't be cleaned, so close this ticket now.
and please continue https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/120298
thanks.

Hi @rxwang662001 , as I asked above, for the secret that was cleaned, have you added the secret name to the service account? (There is a Secrets field in the service account, if added, the secret name will be in the Secrets list of the service account) This is important, as for the manually created secrets, their names will not be in the service account field, only the automatcially created secrets will be. Through this way, we differentiate the auto-generated secrets and manually created secrets. We only want to clean the auto-generated secrets, but not the manually created ones. Thank you very much!

title: Node Graceful Shutdown is taking too long
body:
### What happened?

Pods usually have a 30s grace period when they do not define a terminationGracePeriodSeconds for termination. When NodeGraceful Shutdown is enabled the grace period gets set to the ShutdownGracePeriodSeconds, which is configured by the Kubelet. Let's say the Kubelet is configured with a ShutdownGracePeriodSeconds of 65 minutes. This means that pods without a termination grace period can terminate with a grace period of 65 minutes.

The Kubelet configuration includes:

```
...
shutdownGracePeriod: 65m
shutdownGracePeriodCriticalPods: 35m
```

alternatively, this alternate configuration does not work either:
```
...
shutdownGracePeriodByPodPriority:
  - priority: 0
    shutdownGracePeriodSeconds: 300
  - priority: 10000
    shutdownGracePeriodSeconds: 600
  - priority: 2000000000
    shutdownGracePeriodSeconds: 1200
  - priority: 2000001000
    shutdownGracePeriodSeconds: 1200
```

The Kubernetes E2E tests timeout when this configuration is applied as the default, since many E2E tests and pods do not set a terminationGracePeriodSeconds field.

The fix is to set the [graceful termination](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/dd6bc2548e008e5d49a62dff73af1aa18712a1cb/pkg/kubelet/nodeshutdown/nodeshutdown_manager_linux.go#L368C1-L368C1) to 30 seconds by default, and allow the shutdown code to override the [grace period](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/dd6bc2548e008e5d49a62dff73af1aa18712a1cb/pkg/kubelet/nodeshutdown/nodeshutdown_manager_linux.go#L372) if the pod sets one.

### What did you expect to happen?

I expect pods without a terminationGracePeriodSeconds to be terminated after 30 seconds with a large `shutdownGracePeriod` set within Kubelet.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Configure Kubelet with this config:

```
...
shutdownGracePeriod: 65m
shutdownGracePeriodCriticalPods: 35m
```

Create a pod without a terminationGracePeriodSeconds and observe the 65m grace period used.

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

Hi @rphillips 

Thank you for bringing up this issue regarding Node Graceful Shutdown. The behavior you've described—where pods inherit an excessively long grace period from the Kubelet's shutdownGracePeriod—does seem problematic, especially for E2E tests.

Possible Solutions
Default to 30s Grace Period Unless Explicitly Set: The Kubelet could be modified to enforce a 30-second default grace period for pod termination unless the pod explicitly sets a terminationGracePeriodSeconds. This would align with the expected behavior you've described.

Explicitly Set terminationGracePeriodSeconds in Critical Pods: As a workaround, critical or high-priority pods could explicitly set this field to ensure they get the desired behavior.

Update E2E Tests: To deal with test timeouts, the E2E tests could be updated to explicitly set a terminationGracePeriodSeconds that fits within the test timeout period.

Next Steps
Open a PR or further discuss this in an existing one to reach consensus on the best path forward.
If the first solution is agreed upon, contribute a fix where the Kubelet defaults to a 30-second grace period for pods that don't specify terminationGracePeriodSeconds.
Validate the fix with unit tests and E2E tests to ensure it behaves as expected.

title: Transient Driver Registration on the CSINode can Result in Missed NodeUnstageVolume RPCs During Pod Migration
body:
### What happened?

In `unmountDetachDevices` (see [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/03126c5465879491be33d5064e6f6f1c4ff2a276/pkg/kubelet/volumemanager/reconciler/reconciler_common.go#L279-L316)) we have the following code that will ultimately dispatch `NodeUnstageVolume` RPCs to the underlying CSI plugin.

Here is a pseudo-code representation of the current logic:

```
function unmountDetachDevices
	for all unmounted volumes in ASoW
		if volume not in DSoW &&
		   not operation pending on volume
			if device is mounted globally or
			   device is mounted uncertain
				Case A:
				unmount device
				(this will kick off the NodeUnstageVolume RPC; we want to be here)
			else
				Case B:
				just remove volume from ASoW
				(general badness since we don't issue a NodeUnstageVolume RPC)
```

In our testbeds, we have observed a number of occurrences where we fall into `Case B` when the CSI Node plugin for a particular driver is being bounced, which leads to the volumemanager failing to dispatch the `NodeUnstageVolume` RPC. If the pod migrates to another node, this will leave behind a Zombie LUN in our testbeds (we're using iSCSI).

A Zombie LUN can and often does result in corruption when other pods later migrate to the node in question.

Based on testing that we conducted, we discovered that this case occurs because the device is marked as unmounted.

Initially, we see the device marked as uncertain during reconstruction.

However, if the CSI Node driver pod is bounced in the exact window when a `NodeStageVolume` RPC is issued, then we end up [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/03126c5465879491be33d5064e6f6f1c4ff2a276/pkg/volume/util/operationexecutor/operation_generator.go#L777C1-L798C2).

There we check to see if the error encountered is a “transient error” or a “final error”; if a “final error” is encountered, then the device state transitions from uncertain to unmounted. That is what is happening in our case.

The error is generated when the CSIClient cannot find the requested driver [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/03126c5465879491be33d5064e6f6f1c4ff2a276/pkg/volume/csi/csi_client.go#L158C1-L161C3).

The driver registration code is socket based; based on our testing, if the Node plugin goes down for any reason the driver registration is removed from the CSINode.

Now for the `NodePublishVolume` path, this is mitigated by wrapping the error in a transient error [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/03126c5465879491be33d5064e6f6f1c4ff2a276/pkg/volume/csi/csi_mounter.go#L109C3-L109C3) (I assume to avoid such state transitions?):

```
	csi, err := c.csiClientGetter.Get()
	if err != nil {
		return volumetypes.NewTransientOperationFailure(log("mounter.SetUpAt failed to get CSI client: %v", err))
	}
```

Based on our testing to date, adding parity [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/03126c5465879491be33d5064e6f6f1c4ff2a276/pkg/volume/csi/csi_attacher.go#L290) to the `NodeStageVolume` path would help us avoid Zombie LUNs in our test setups due to missing `NodeUnstageVolume` calls:

```
	// lets check if node/unstage is supported
	if c.csiClient == nil {
		c.csiClient, err = newCsiDriverClient(csiDriverName(csiSource.Driver))
		if err != nil {
			return errors.New(log("attacher.MountDevice failed to create newCsiDriverClient: %v", err))
		}
	}
	csi := c.csiClient
```

This can be fixed by also wrapping this error in a transient error.

### What did you expect to happen?

We expected to see a `NodeUnstageVolume` call coming to the underlying NodePlugin (once it was finally back up).

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

* Force reconstruction on a node.
* Take down the CSI node plugin on the node while pods are mounting.
* Try to migrate the pod to another node; the underlying machinery will correctly wait for the plugin to come back up before proceeding.
* Later, bring up the CSI node plugin.
* While the pod migration might be successful, a `NodeUnstageVolume` should be missing if the correct timing windows were hit.

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

title: App container is started before initContainers could complete on node reboot
body:
### What happened?

On node reboot, we see app container is started before initContainers could complete. Essentially both app and initContainers are running in parallel. We are using initContainers to ensure dependent drivers are loaded by other pod before the app container could start. But because app container is starting in parallel, they hit a failure. This was not seen with k8s 1.27 and only happening with 1.28. Also, this happens only on node reboot, not during fresh install of our application (gpu-operator)

confirmed that this is NOT reproduced in 1.27. It is a regression.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/3cf3702d1e638548ba9fcfd957ebae43e1a573cb/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_container.go#L886-L890

This happens because the kubelet uses the old container statuses to check if the pod has been initialized before.

Before 1.28, the kubelet considers the pod as initialized if there is any regular container running.
However, with 1.28, the kubelet considers the pod as initialized if there is any regular container running OR EXITED.

I think the latter one is theoretically right, but currently, we cannot know if the container statuses are from the current pod sandbox or the old one.

The fix would be,
1. check if the container statuses are outdated (not sure how to do this yet...)
2. (workaround) revert pod initialization check: there is any regular container running or exited => there is any regular container running

that looks to have changed as part of sidecar work - there were a *lot* of changes to pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_container.go in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/116429/files#diff-d86ffc24d8e4c9deafd3e39e8f4ee3546ee46a31dcea8ea6526443b3f4bffa28 that are not obviously feature gated... were *all* of those supposed to be no-op refactors?

> The fix would be,
> 
> 1. check if the container statuses are outdated (not sure how to do this yet...)
> 2. (workaround) revert pod initialization check: there is any regular container running or exited => there is any regular container running

A starting point that would build confidence would be to restore the kubelet logic here to the 1.27 state before the sidecar merge (reviewing `diff(release-1.27, Fix PR)` should make it obvious that 1.27 behavior has been restored).

The refactored / new methods could be kept in a different file and only called when the feature gate was enabled. That would restore 1.28 to match 1.27 behavior by default as quickly as possible.

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

This will address the #120247 with feature gate disabled.

```

index 3fd849e4ae2..97abc229335 100644

+++ b/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_container.go

@@ -136,7 +137,6 @@ func calcRestartCountByLogDir(path string) (int, error) {

@@ -144,6 +144,7 @@ func calcRestartCountByLogDir(path string) (int, error) {

 	}
+	restartCount := 0
 	restartCountLogFileRegex := regexp.MustCompile(`^(\d+)\.log(\..*)?`)
 	for _, file := range files {

@@ -328,7 +329,7 @@ func (m *kubeGenericRuntimeManager) generateContainerConfig(ctx context.Context,

-		Image:       &runtimeapi.ImageSpec{Image: imageRef},
+		Image:       &runtimeapi.ImageSpec{Image: imageRef, UserSpecifiedImage: container.Image},

@@ -725,19 +726,21 @@ func (m *kubeGenericRuntimeManager) killContainer(ctx context.Context, pod *v1.P
 	}
 	m.recordContainerEvent(pod, containerSpec, containerID.ID, v1.EventTypeNormal, events.KillingContainer, message)
 
+	if gracePeriodOverride != nil {

-	if gracePeriodOverride != nil {
-		gracePeriod = *gracePeriodOverride
-		klog.V(3).InfoS("Killing container with a grace period override", "pod", klog.KObj(pod), "podUID", pod.UID,
-			"containerName", containerName, "containerID", containerID.String(), "gracePeriod", gracePeriod)
-	}
 
 	klog.V(2).InfoS("Killing container with a grace period", "pod", klog.KObj(pod), "podUID", pod.UID,
 		"containerName", containerName, "containerID", containerID.String(), "gracePeriod", gracePeriod)
@@ -903,6 +906,230 @@ func findNextInitContainerToRun(pod *v1.Pod, podStatus *kubecontainer.PodStatus)
 	return nil, &pod.Spec.InitContainers[0], false
 }
 
+// hasAnyRegularContainerCreated returns true if any regular container has been
+// created, which indicates all init containers have been initialized.
+func hasAnyRegularContainerCreated(pod *v1.Pod, podStatus *kubecontainer.PodStatus) bool {
+	for _, container := range pod.Spec.Containers {
+		status := podStatus.FindContainerStatusByName(container.Name)
+		if status == nil {
+			continue
+		}
+		switch status.State {
+		case kubecontainer.ContainerStateCreated,
+			kubecontainer.ContainerStateRunning,
+			kubecontainer.ContainerStateExited:
+			return true
+		default:
+			// Ignore other states
+		}
+	}
+	return false
+}
+
+// computeInitContainerActions sets the actions on the given changes that need
+// to be taken for the init containers. This includes actions to initialize the
+// init containers and actions to keep restartable init containers running.
+// computeInitContainerActions returns true if pod has been initialized.
+//
+// The actions include:
+// - Start the first init container that has not been started.
+// - Restart all restartable init containers that have started but are not running.
+// - Kill the restartable init containers that are not alive or started.
+//
+// Note that this is a function for the SidecarContainers feature.
+// Please sync with the findNextInitContainerToRun function if any changes are
+// made, as either this or that function will be called.
+func (m *kubeGenericRuntimeManager) computeInitContainerActions(pod *v1.Pod, podStatus *kubecontainer.PodStatus, changes *podActions) bool {
+	if len(pod.Spec.InitContainers) == 0 {
+		return true
+	}
+
+	// If any of the main containers have status and are Running, then all init containers must
+	// have been executed at some point in the past.  However, they could have been removed
+	// from the container runtime now, and if we proceed, it would appear as if they
+	// never ran and will re-execute improperly except for the restartable init containers.
+	podHasInitialized := hasAnyRegularContainerCreated(pod, podStatus)
+
+	// isPreviouslyInitialized indicates if the current init container is
+	// previously initialized.
+	isPreviouslyInitialized := podHasInitialized
+	restartOnFailure := shouldRestartOnFailure(pod)
+
+	// Note that we iterate through the init containers in reverse order to find
+	// the next init container to run, as the completed init containers may get
+	// removed from container runtime for various reasons. Therefore the kubelet
+	// should rely on the minimal number of init containers - the last one.
+	//
+	// Once we find the next init container to run, iterate through the rest to
+	// find the restartable init containers to restart.
+	for i := len(pod.Spec.InitContainers) - 1; i >= 0; i-- {
+		container := &pod.Spec.InitContainers[i]
+		status := podStatus.FindContainerStatusByName(container.Name)
+		klog.V(4).InfoS("Computing init container action", "pod", klog.KObj(pod), "container", container.Name, "status", status)
+		if status == nil {
+			// If the container is previously initialized but its status is not
+			// found, it means its last status is removed for some reason.
+			// Restart it if it is a restartable init container.
+			if isPreviouslyInitialized && types.IsRestartableInitContainer(container) {
+				changes.InitContainersToStart = append(changes.InitContainersToStart, i)
+			}
+			continue
+		}
+
+		if isPreviouslyInitialized && !types.IsRestartableInitContainer(container) {
+			// after initialization, only restartable init containers need to be kept
+			// running
+			continue
+		}
+
+		switch status.State {
+		case kubecontainer.ContainerStateCreated:
+			// nothing to do but wait for it to start
+
+		case kubecontainer.ContainerStateRunning:
+			if !types.IsRestartableInitContainer(container) {
+				break
+			}
+
+			if types.IsRestartableInitContainer(container) {
+				if container.StartupProbe != nil {
+					startup, found := m.startupManager.Get(status.ID)
+					if !found {
+						// If the startup probe has not been run, wait for it.
+						break
+					}
+					if startup != proberesults.Success {
+						if startup == proberesults.Failure {
+							// If the restartable init container failed the startup probe,
+							// restart it.
+							changes.ContainersToKill[status.ID] = containerToKillInfo{
+								name:      container.Name,
+								container: container,
+								message:   fmt.Sprintf("Init container %s failed startup probe", container.Name),
+								reason:    reasonStartupProbe,
+							}
+							changes.InitContainersToStart = append(changes.InitContainersToStart, i)
+						}
+						break
+					}
+				}
+
+				klog.V(4).InfoS("Init container has been initialized", "pod", klog.KObj(pod), "container", container.Name)
+				if i == (len(pod.Spec.InitContainers) - 1) {
+					podHasInitialized = true
+				} else if !isPreviouslyInitialized {
+					// this init container is initialized for the first time, start the next one
+					changes.InitContainersToStart = append(changes.InitContainersToStart, i+1)
+				}
+
+				// A restartable init container does not have to take into account its
+				// liveness probe when it determines to start the next init container.
+				if container.LivenessProbe != nil {
+					liveness, found := m.livenessManager.Get(status.ID)
+					if !found {
+						// If the liveness probe has not been run, wait for it.
+						break
+					}
+					if liveness == proberesults.Failure {
+						// If the restartable init container failed the liveness probe,
+						// restart it.
+						changes.ContainersToKill[status.ID] = containerToKillInfo{
+							name:      container.Name,
+							container: container,
+							message:   fmt.Sprintf("Init container %s failed liveness probe", container.Name),
+							reason:    reasonLivenessProbe,
+						}
+						changes.InitContainersToStart = append(changes.InitContainersToStart, i)
+					}
+				}
+			} else { // init container
+				// nothing do to but wait for it to finish
+				break
+			}
+
+		// If the init container failed and the restart policy is Never, the pod is terminal.
+		// Otherwise, restart the init container.
+		case kubecontainer.ContainerStateExited:
+			if types.IsRestartableInitContainer(container) {
+				changes.InitContainersToStart = append(changes.InitContainersToStart, i)
+			} else { // init container
+				if isInitContainerFailed(status) {
+					if !restartOnFailure {
+						changes.KillPod = true
+						changes.InitContainersToStart = nil
+						return false
+					}
+					changes.InitContainersToStart = append(changes.InitContainersToStart, i)
+					break
+				}
+

ok, but thing is: kubelet is supposed to log when it is about to change this setting: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.22/pkg/kubelet/cm/cpumanager/cpu_manager.go#L467

1.22 already includes an optimization for which the cpumanager reconcile loop will skip containers whose cpuset is not changed since last update. The key assumption is that the kubelet is the exclusive owner of cpuset cgroup though. If there is any external agent which changes this setting, the results are unpredictable.

In #107471, I added a bunch of unit tests to the iptables proxy which parse the outputs from the Proxier so we can then have tests like:

```
	runPacketFlowTests(t, getLine(), ipt, testNodeIP, []packetFlowTest{
		{
			name:     "cluster IP accepted",
			sourceIP: "10.180.0.2",
			destIP:   "172.30.0.41",
			destPort: 80,
			output:   "10.180.0.1:80",
			masq:     false,
		},
		{
			name:     "hairpin to cluster IP",
			sourceIP: "10.180.0.1",
			destIP:   "172.30.0.41",
			destPort: 80,
			output:   "10.180.0.1:80",
			masq:     true,
		},
	})
```

ie, that tests that according to the current state of the iptables rules in `ipt`, that
- a packet from 10.180.0.2 to 172.30.0.41:80 should be NATted to 10.180.0.1:80 without masquerading
- a packet from 10.180.0.1 to 172.30.0.41:80 should be NATted to 10.180.0.1:80 _with_ masquerading"

I'd like to abstract these a bit and try to share them between the different backends. (In particular, for my work on the nftables backend, I'd like to make sure I'm testing all of the same cases as the iptables tests are.)

I'm envisioning something where like you'd have a unit test that creates a Proxier and a "flow test runner" of the right type for your backend, and then you call something like `proxytesting.TestClusterIP(t, proxier, flowTestRunner)`, and that centralized function calls `OnServiceAdded`, `OnEndpointSliceAdded`, etc, on the proxier to set up the state, then uses the flow test runner object to test out various scenarios like the ones above to make sure they give the right results. And by having these tests in a central shared directory, we'd have more closely-aligned test cases in the different proxies...

Anyway, this is still probably a ways off, but if you implement something like #107471 in winkernel then I (or someone else) can try to pull it into a larger abstraction later...

title: Evicting Pod due to emptyDir violation returns as Completed
body:
### What happened?

If a Pod is evicted because it violates EmptyDir storage limits, your pod will be evicted but it will be marked as completed.  



### What did you expect to happen?

I would expect the pod to say `terminating` or `Failed` rather than completed.  For a Job, the controller will take this Pod to be succeeded even though it was evicted.  

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Run the K8 job below.

```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: emptydir-job
spec:
  backoffLimit: 1  # Number of retries before considering the Job as failed
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
        - name: emptydir-container
          image: nginx
          volumeMounts:
            - name: emptydir-volume
              mountPath: /data
      volumes:
      - name: emptydir-volume
        emptyDir:
         sizeLimit: 500Mi
```

I exec into this pod and run `fallocate -l 1 Gb /data/dummy.txt`

If you wait a few seconds, the pod will be evicted.

### Anything else we need to know?

It doesn't seem to matter if this is a naked pod or not.  For a job, this is especially bad as it would be considered a successful run.  



### Kubernetes version

Current main.

# paste output here

title: Kube-proxy setting (with proxy-mode being ipvs) ipvs.udpTimeout doesn't work
body:
### What happened? #84041 Introduced a way to control timeouts for UDP traffic when kube-proxy works in IPVS mode. The setting simply doesn't work, making the actual timeout value get inherited from the underlying system configuration `net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_udp_timeout` (being 30sec by default). ### What did you expect to happen? The setting for kube-proxy should 'beat' the system value. ### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)? Via kube-proxy configmap set `mode: ipvs` and `ipvs.udpTimeout: 300s`. Restart kube-proxy DaemonSet for settings to supposedly take effect. Test by sending UDP traffic via kubernetes Service and observe the actual timeouts in conntrack table. ### Anything else we need to know? The mechanism seems to be majorly broken: `ipvs.syncPeriod` option seems to wipe all entries about related UDP connections **regardless** of their current timeout timer value in the conntrack table! I.e. a connection with, say, 20s of time left before timeout occurs - will get wiped upon kube-proxy's sync! ### Kubernetes version

@aroradaman I got a bit closer to the issue:
So on a kubernetes cluster v1.25.5 everything seems to work perfectly:
I now see entries about my UDP traffic on the correct node.
The timeout there matches the value set via kube-proxy ConfigMap.
The entry about my UDP connection doesn't get wiped before it's timeout timer reaches 0 (so, the behavior here is correct) neither from IPVS nor from conntrack tables.

Re-testing now on v1.26.3 cluster where I see the problem and trying to diff options between these 2 clusters.

Well, that's weird, but on the cluster where I initially caught the problem (v1.26.3) I clearly see kube-proxy being configured with `mode: ipvs` (I even restarted kube-proxy DaemonSet just to make sure what I see in the ConfigMap is what is actually applied), but when I send UDP traffic - I only see an entry about it in conntrack table, but nothing about any UDP at all in IPVS table.
I test it the very same way I tested on v1.25.5.
I am puzzled now.

Edit:
I've tested on another cluster (v1.26.2), but there's no kube-proxy and thus UDP connections appears neither in conntrack nor in IPVS there, but I guess, that's expected behavior for a cluster without kube-proxy (CNI: Calico)?

As @aroradaman I can't see that any conntrack entries are removed on a kube-proxy sync. I _can_ confirm that an UDP "connection" fails when the conntrack entry times out (default 30s or 120s if ASSURED).

Since ipvs preserves it's entry, the conntrack should be re-created even when it has expired when a new packet arrives. That has worked in the past, but is broken by `--random-fully`. Now, when the conntrack entry expires the next packet will get a new random source port that the server knows nothing about.

I tested to re-build kube-proxy without `--random-fully` and then everything works fine. The conntrack entry is re-created with the same addr/port as for the original packet.

`--random-fully` can probably not be removed, but can perhaps be made configurable in some way. Some servers may actually expect the original client source port to be preserved (for UDP and SCTP that is, but not likely for TCP)

@Drugoy  If you can live with `externalTrafficPolicy: Local` for your service (assuming your traffic is from an external client) that is a work-around. Then the source port and source address are preserved (no `--random-fully`).

Seems like a good idea. Since that is the only way for proxy-mode=iptables, I wonder why it's missing

@aroradaman @uablrek thank you!
To sum it up:
1. it looks like I have 1 weird cluster where kube-proxy is configured to work in IPVS mode, but UDP connections for some reason don't get into IPVS table. This behavior doesn't reproduce at least on 1 another cluster (though their versions are different) on my end and on @aroradaman's cluster. This behavior looks like a bug, but is different from what I've initially described in this ticket.
2. @uablrek provided a workaround (either use `externalTrafficPolicy: Local` in the Service or re-build kube-proxy without `--random-fully`) for my case that should re-create iptables entry based on IPVS entry if only IPVS timeouts were configured and netfilter's timeouts remain with default values.
3. It looks like there's a case for Feature Request to add a proxy configuration for `config.Conntrack.UDPTimeout` option. Would you like me to file this as a separate ticket?

Now even though a workaround might suit my case, I'd still like to understand why one of my cluster behaves so that sending UDP traffic doesn't result into an entry in IPVS table, while kube-proxy's is clearly configured to work in IPVS mode.
I think this is the reason why kube-proxy's `ipvs.syncPeriod` timer wipes the entries from conntrack table.
I will try to investigate that on my own, but I'd appreciate any help/hints/explanations. My only suspicion is that it has something to do with CNI (Calico) configuration. I just learned that kube-proxy is basically optional and we even have 1 cluster working without it at all.
@Drugoy feel free to open an issue for adding conntrack.UDPTimeout configuration.

This behavior doesn't reproduce at least on 1 another cluster (though their versions are different) on my end and on @aroradaman's cluster. This behavior looks like a bug, but is different from what I've initially described in this ticket.

Kubernetes does not set ipvs timeouts directly. It rely on this: https://github.com/moby/ipvs/blob/master/netlink_linux.go#L602 (netlink wrapper). The failure can be specific to your setup. Can you check kernel logs via `dmesg`?

otherwise, we should surface UDP conntrack settings to config.

title: Namespace stuck in Terminating when deleted if ApiService doesn't implement Aggregated Discovery
body:
### What happened?

We implement a manual `APIService` API Extension in [Agones](https://github.com/googleforgames/agones).

Definition:
https://github.com/googleforgames/agones/blob/main/install/helm/agones/templates/service/allocation.yaml

Code for handling web requests:
https://github.com/googleforgames/agones/blob/main/pkg/util/apiserver/apiserver.go

The code is extremely lightweight as we only have no need for storage, and only accept CREATE requests at this time.

This issue was first reported by one of our users in May, but we only were able to reproduce it ourselves once we were on 1.27.x: https://github.com/googleforgames/agones/issues/3172

Testing on Kubernetes 1.27.x we noticed that when attempting to delete Namespaces, they would get stuck in termination with the following description:

```
❯ kubectl describe ns 1690585578
Name:         1690585578
Labels:       kubernetes.io/metadata.name=1690585578
              owner=e2e-test
Annotations:  <none>
Status:       Terminating
Conditions:
  Type                                         Status  LastTransitionTime               Reason                  Message
  ----                                         ------  ------------------               ------                  -------
  NamespaceDeletionDiscoveryFailure            True    Fri, 28 Jul 2023 16:07:44 -0700  DiscoveryFailed         Discovery failed for some groups, 1 failing: unable to retrieve the complete list of server APIs: allocation.agones.dev/v1: stale GroupVersion discovery: allocation.agones.dev/v1
  NamespaceDeletionGroupVersionParsingFailure  False   Fri, 28 Jul 2023 16:07:46 -0700  ParsedGroupVersions     All legacy kube types successfully parsed
  NamespaceDeletionContentFailure              False   Fri, 28 Jul 2023 16:08:56 -0700  ContentDeleted          All content successfully deleted, may be waiting on finalization
  NamespaceContentRemaining                    False   Fri, 28 Jul 2023 16:08:56 -0700  ContentRemoved          All content successfully removed
  NamespaceFinalizersRemaining                 False   Fri, 28 Jul 2023 16:08:56 -0700  ContentHasNoFinalizers  All content-preserving finalizers finished
```

So far, I've not found a way to delete the Namespace.

Looking through the log for the webserver, i can see requests for `/apis` and the new Aggregated Discovery feature (`Accept:  "application/json;g=apidiscovery.k8s.io;v=v2beta1;as=APIGroupDiscoveryList"`), but we return a 404 to that response, since it's not implemented.

Looking through the code I can find (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.27.3/staging/src/k8s.io/kube-aggregator/pkg/apiserver/handler_discovery.go) it seems that any response other than `http.StatusOK` would result in this issue -- which is breaking backward compatibility within `APIService` to assume that this API surface is implemented in some way.


### What did you expect to happen?

Namespaces would terminate as per normal.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Install Agones on a cluster (https://agones.dev/site/docs/installation/install-agones/)
2. `kubectl create ns foo`
3. `kubectl delete ns foo`
4. Watch as the ns gets stuck in Terminating.



### Anything else we need to know?

If I had a magic wand, I'd love a reference of all the API's that get called against an APIService and what their expected results should be.

So far it's a combo of using `kubectl proxy` and looking at the k8s API responses, crawling through code, and reading apiserver logs to try and reverse engineer this work.

Something else I also just noticed -- there are no errors or events that pertain to this issue attached to the `APIService` either, which would be useful for debugging if it were.

```

Will edit this comment as we go, but just writing down some useful notes:

- agones should support the `/apis` endpoint: https://github.com/googleforgames/agones/blob/main/pkg/util/apiserver/apiserver.go#L130 so it's weird that a 404 is required
- Aggregated Discovery is fully backwards compatible with previous versions. A fallback https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.27.3/staging/src/k8s.io/kube-aggregator/pkg/apiserver/handler_discovery.go#L231-L233 is implemented so not supporting aggregated discovery on an APIService will fall back to the old behavior (without the `Accept:  "application/json;g=apidiscovery.k8s.io;v=v2beta1;as=APIGroupDiscoveryList"` accept header)
- The issue brought up https://github.com/googleforgames/agones/issues/3172 is on v1.26.5 in which aggregated discovery is disabled (only enabled for 1.27+)

> * Aggregated Discovery is fully backwards compatible with previous versions. A fallback https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.27.3/staging/src/k8s.io/kube-aggregator/pkg/apiserver/handler_discovery.go#L231-L233 is implemented so not supporting aggregated discovery on an APIService will fall back to the old behavior (without the `Accept:  "application/json;g=apidiscovery.k8s.io;v=v2beta1;as=APIGroupDiscoveryList"` accept header)

That assumes the aggregated server is paying attention to the Accept header, and will respond with a NotAcceptable status code if it doesn't support aggregated discovery... that may or may not be true... ways we could make that stronger / more compatible:
1. double check the response content-type
2. send a single request to `/apis` that indicates it accepts BOTH `application/json` and `application/json;g=apidiscovery.k8s.io;v=v2beta1;as=APIGroupDiscoveryList`, and use the content-type in the returned data to decide whether to go down the aggregated or normal discovery path


 ideally, it would make a single request that indicated it accepted

Thanks to an offline chat with @Jefftree - can confirm that returning `HTTP: 406` from `/apis` resolved the issue!

Long term we'll look at implementing Aggregate Discovery, but this at least gets us past the initial hurdle. Thanks for the support!

> Thanks to an offline chat with @Jefftree - can confirm that returning `HTTP: 406` from `/apis` resolved the issue!

to be clear, this is returning a 406 to requests that don't accept `application/json`, right?

ah, right... the non-aggregated discovery calls directly to `/apis/$group/$version`

@Jefftree to be actually compatible, I think the "success case" for aggregated discovery should check that the status code is `200` and the returned content is actually aggregated discovery json, and if either of those are false, it should fall back to non-aggregated discovery.

> ah, right... the non-aggregated discovery calls directly to `/apis/$group/$version`
> 
> @Jefftree to be actually compatible, I think the "success case" for aggregated discovery should check that the status code is `200` and the returned content-type is aggregated discovery json, and if either of those are false, it should fall back to non-aggregated discovery.

Yeah I agree, we made a couple assumptions based on the sample apiserver that could be improved for stronger compatibility guarantees. Will look into sending a PR for this once code freeze is over.

/triage accepted
/assign

    "type": "Hostname"
  }
]
```

With primary ipFamily="IPv6", the kube-proxy `bindAddress` seem to be used:
```
I0723 11:40:33.843305     366 proxier.go:405] "Record nodeIP and family" nodeIP="0.0.0.0" family="IPv4"
I0723 11:40:33.843392     366 proxier.go:405] "Record nodeIP and family" nodeIP="::1" family="IPv6"
```

/sig network
/area kube-proxy

### What did you expect to happen?

The nodeIP address for the correct family as configured in the node object should be passed as `nodeIP` to kube-proxiers

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Start `kube-proxy` with log-level >=2 and grep the logs for:
```
"Record nodeIP and family"
```

### Anything else we need to know?

The `nodeIP` seem to be used in just one place in both proxiers:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d0814fa476c72201dcc599297171fe65fb657908/pkg/proxy/ipvs/proxier.go#L1227-L1230

`allowFromNode` will be false for an unspecified (any) address regardless of the *real* nodeIP..

I wanted to use `nodeIP` as "src" for routes, that's how I discovered this problem, but in any case, nodeIP should be correct

### Kubernetes version

v1.27.4 and master

### Cloud provider

N/A

### OS version

N/A

### Install tools

None

### Container runtime (CRI) and version (if applicable)

crio version 1.27.0


### Related plugins (CNI, CSI, ...) and versions (if applicable)
