nodes.body:
To use the `bindAddress` was intentional, but for dual-stack that only gives one address.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d0814fa476c72201dcc599297171fe65fb657908/cmd/kube-proxy/app/server.go#L915-L919

### Proxy-mode=iptables

Proxier.nodeIP is only used to determine `allowFromNode`

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/97c7dbcd227ec253bb277a91575706fe30f519dc/pkg/proxy/iptables/proxier.go#L1306-L1328

`cidr.Contains()` return "false" for an unspecified address, so for the "secondary" family the additional rule is never added. If the nodeIP is localhost, it *should* never cause allowFromNode=true since it's pointless to add localhost (127.0.0.0/8) in `loadBalancerSourceRanges` (a packet localhost->loadBalancerIP would be a "martian").

So the *only* case when the additional rule is added (allowFromNode=true) is when a loadBalancerSourceRange contains a "real" nodeIP. To allow the bindAddress to possibly override the nodeIP may feel tempting, but the bindAddress is usually configured in the config-file (or configMap), so it's very hard for normal K8s users to set it "per-node".

The additional rule in only needed if the loadBalancerIP is also assigned to a local interface on the node. I think that's rare for proxy-mode=iptables, so I think that's why nobody have encountered this bug.

### Proxy-mode=ipvs

The loadBalancerIP's are **always** added to `kube-ipvs0` so the `allowFromNode` thing as in proxy-mode=iptables isn't feasible. It may be removed.

On the other hand, for proxy-mode=ipvs you can't restrict access to the loadBalancerIP from the node with `loadBalancerSourceRanges`!

So a better alternative may be to use it "the other way around": block access unless allowFromNode=true. But that should be another issue (and PR)
/triage accepted
/assign @uablrek

nodes.title: Kube-proxy: Get nodeIPs for both families with dual-stack
nodes.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug
/sig network
/area kube-proxy



#### What this PR does / why we need it:

For kube-proxy in dual-stack mode the `nodeIP` was only set for the primary family, while the other got an "any" address. This PR uses the nodeIPs in the node object (if possible)

#### Which issue(s) this PR fixes:

Fixes #119524

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

~The "bindAddress" no longer have precedence over the nodeIP in the K8s node object, but is only used as fallback. It is the way it should be IMO, and shouldn't have any backward compatibility issues since the nodeIP is only used at one place in the proxiers (so far).~

The "bindAddress" overrides an address in the node object if it's specified and not the "any" address or a loopback address.

The returned nodeIPs are never an "any" address (zeroes), if the address can't be read from the node object, localhost (127.0.0.1 or ::1) is returned.

The log printouts mentioned in #119524 looks like this with this PR:
```
I0723 17:13:56.934852     360 proxier.go:405] "Record nodeIP and family" nodeIP="192.168.1.2" family="IPv4"
I0723 17:13:56.934997     360 proxier.go:405] "Record nodeIP and family" nodeIP="fd00::c0a8:102" family="IPv6"
```

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
The `--bind-address` parameter in kube-proxy is misleading, no port is opened with this address. Instead it is translated internally to "nodeIP". The nodeIPs for both families are now taken from the Node object if `--bind-address` is unspecified or set to the "any" address (0.0.0.0 or ::). It is recommended to leave `--bind-address` unspecified, and in particular avoid to set it to localhost (127.0.0.1 or ::1)
```

You're right, with  `pod.spec.terminationGracePeriod: 0` the pod gets force deleted without unmount confirmation from kubelet. That's unexpected and bad. Even with 1 second of `terminationGracePeriod`, the Pod is not deleted until all its volumes are unmounted, with 0 it's just force deleted without unmounts, potentially corrupting data on mounted volumes. title: Conntrack cleaning happens before network programming endpoints
body:
### What happened?

Currently kube-proxy efficiently cleans all stale conntrack entries preventing traffic black holing for deleted endpoints, but there can be some corner cases when conntrack cleaning happens before programming the network leaving a small window in which if any packet arrives will back-hole the traffic.

The corner case:
Taking a simple case of load-balancer service backed by a deployment with single replica, on deleting the pod(gracefully), I observed two **OnEndpointSliceUpdate** invocations:
1.  First one with EndpointConditions.Ready as false
2. EndpointSlice was cleared for the pod 

The conntrack flow for this case:
1. After processing the first **OnEndpointSliceUpdate** invocation **EndpointsMap** will still have entries for the pod as endpoint still exists, though not in ready state so proxier won't program deletion of endpoint from the data path. But the endpoint IP will be picked for conntrack cleaning as new endpoint != old endpoint because of the not ready condition.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/95e915c4288eda15da1724989f3f7dec9f3512d6/pkg/proxy/endpoints.go#L423-L436
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/95e915c4288eda15da1724989f3f7dec9f3512d6/pkg/proxy/endpoints.go#L120-L126

2.  After processing the second **OnEndpointSliceUpdate** invocation **EndpointsMap** won't have entries for the endpoint and the proxier will program deletion of the endpoint in the data path. EndpointIP won't be picked up for conntrack cleaning as the following logic will skip it
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/95e915c4288eda15da1724989f3f7dec9f3512d6/pkg/proxy/endpoints.go#L417-L421

This behaviour leads to conntrack cleaning one cycle ahead of network programming.  
This might be a regression of https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/106163

### What did you expect to happen?

Conntrack cleanup should happen after programming the network.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

This behaviour can be observed in kube-proxy logs (verbosity=4).
[link to log snippet showing the behaviour](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/119010#issuecomment-1622325495)

I used the following objects for experimenting:
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: test
  labels:
    app: test
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: test

      labels:
        app: test

        args:
          - netexec

        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
---

kind: Service
metadata:
  name: test
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  selector:
    app: test
  ports:
    - protocol: UDP
      name: udp
      nodePort: 31111
      port: 80
      targetPort: 80
```

title: Kubernetes api returns incorrect conflicting fields during server-side apply in some cases
body:
### What happened?

When performing a server-side apply PATCH request, if there are conflicts in what's being applied with differing field owners, kubernetes responds with a 409 conflict error with an array of causes in the error detail, enumerating the conflicting fields that were discovered.

In some cases, we see that the fields returned in this 409 error response are incorrect, containing both duplicate fields, and entirely missing other conflicts.

### What did you expect to happen?

The http 409 error response when receiving a conflict while using server-side apply should contain all of the correct fields (and also ideally no duplicates).

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Save this file as `original.yaml`

<details>

```yaml
kind: DaemonSet
apiVersion: apps/v1
metadata:
  name: simple-probe
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      k8s-app: simple-probe
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        k8s-app: simple-probe
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: probe
        image: registry.k8s.io/busybox
        args:
        - /bin/sh
        - -c
        - touch /tmp/healthy; sleep 9999999
        livenessProbe:
          exec:
            command:
            - cat
            - /tmp/healthy
          periodSeconds: 5
        readinessProbe:
          exec:
            command:
            - cat
            - /tmp/healthy
          periodSeconds: 5
```

</details>

Save this file as `modified.yaml`

<details>

```yaml
kind: DaemonSet
apiVersion: apps/v1
metadata:
  name: simple-probe
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: probe
        livenessProbe:
          exec:
            command:
            - ls
            - /tmp/healthy
          periodSeconds: 10
        readinessProbe:
          exec:
            command:
            - ls
            - /tmp/healthy
          periodSeconds: 10
```

</details>

Now apply the first yaml with server-side apply:

`kubectl apply -f original.yaml --server-side --field-manager=original`

Apply the second yaml with server-side apply, using a different field manager:

`kubectl apply -f modified.yaml --server-side --field-manager=modified --validate=false --force-conflicts`

If we get the applied daemonset at this point (`kubectl get ds simple-probe -o yaml --show-managed-fields`), everything appears to be applied correctly with expected behavior and expected field owners

Now try to re-apply with the original command/field manager, forcing a conflict error to be returned (increased verbosity to see returned http body):

`kubectl apply -f original.yaml --server-side --field-manager=original -v=9`

When re-applying this original yaml (without force-conflicts), we expect to observe conflicts on all of the fields that were changed by modified.yaml and now owned by the `modified` field manager. These _should_ be:
```
.spec.template.spec.containers[name="probe"].livenessProbe.exec.command
.spec.template.spec.containers[name="probe"].livenessProbe.periodSeconds
.spec.template.spec.containers[name="probe"].readinessProbe.exec.command
.spec.template.spec.containers[name="probe"].readinessProbe.periodSeconds
```

However, this is the response we get when trying to apply using the increased verbosity command:

```
I0706 12:56:34.394111   74086 request.go:1188] Request Body: {"apiVersion":"apps/v1","kind":"DaemonSet","metadata":{"name":"simple-probe","namespace":"default"},"spec":{"selector":{"matchLabels":{"k8s-app":"simple-probe"}},"template":{"metadata":{"labels":{"k8s-app":"simple-probe"}},"spec":{"containers":[{"args":["/bin/sh","-c","touch /tmp/healthy; sleep 9999999"],"image":"registry.k8s.io/busybox","livenessProbe":{"exec":{"command":["cat","/tmp/healthy"]},"periodSeconds":5},"name":"probe","readinessProbe":{"exec":{"command":["cat","/tmp/healthy"]},"periodSeconds":5}}]}}}}
I0706 12:56:34.394215   74086 round_trippers.go:466] curl -v -XPATCH  -H "Accept: application/json" -H "Content-Type: application/apply-patch+yaml" -H "User-Agent: kubectl/v1.27.3 (darwin/amd64) kubernetes/25b4e43" 'https://<REDACTED>/apis/apps/v1/namespaces/default/daemonsets/simple-probe?fieldManager=original&fieldValidation=Strict&force=false'
I0706 12:56:34.408095   74086 round_trippers.go:553] PATCH https://<REDACTED>/apis/apps/v1/namespaces/default/daemonsets/simple-probe?fieldManager=original&fieldValidation=Strict&force=false 409 Conflict in 13 milliseconds
I0706 12:56:34.408123   74086 round_trippers.go:570] HTTP Statistics: GetConnection 0 ms ServerProcessing 13 ms Duration 13 ms
I0706 12:56:34.408133   74086 round_trippers.go:577] Response Headers:
I0706 12:56:34.408142   74086 round_trippers.go:580]     Date: Thu, 06 Jul 2023 19:56:34 GMT
I0706 12:56:34.408147   74086 round_trippers.go:580]     Audit-Id: 4d2e7d6c-109c-4fb5-93eb-e81d5a4c9ead
I0706 12:56:34.408152   74086 round_trippers.go:580]     Cache-Control: no-cache, private
I0706 12:56:34.408157   74086 round_trippers.go:580]     Content-Type: application/json
I0706 12:56:34.408162   74086 round_trippers.go:580]     X-Kubernetes-Pf-Flowschema-Uid: 4fe5247d-d953-4884-81cc-c1abf9bd2989
I0706 12:56:34.408167   74086 round_trippers.go:580]     X-Kubernetes-Pf-Prioritylevel-Uid: 35c473fc-8e57-4244-9c7f-788f96aa29fd
I0706 12:56:34.408305   74086 round_trippers.go:580]     Content-Length: 1107
I0706 12:56:34.408342   74086 request.go:1188] Response Body: {"kind":"Status","apiVersion":"v1","metadata":{},"status":"Failure","message":"Apply failed with 4 conflicts: conflicts with \"modified\":\n- .spec.template.spec.containers[name=\"probe\"].readinessProbe.exec\n- .spec.template.spec.containers[name=\"probe\"].readinessProbe.exec.command\n- .spec.template.spec.containers[name=\"probe\"].readinessProbe.exec\n- .spec.template.spec.containers[name=\"probe\"].readinessProbe.exec.command","reason":"Conflict","details":{"causes":[{"reason":"FieldManagerConflict","message":"conflict with \"modified\"","field":".spec.template.spec.containers[name=\"probe\"].readinessProbe.exec"},{"reason":"FieldManagerConflict","message":"conflict with \"modified\"","field":".spec.template.spec.containers[name=\"probe\"].readinessProbe.exec.command"},{"reason":"FieldManagerConflict","message":"conflict with \"modified\"","field":".spec.template.spec.containers[name=\"probe\"].readinessProbe.exec"},{"reason":"FieldManagerConflict","message":"conflict with \"modified\"","field":".spec.template.spec.containers[name=\"probe\"].readinessProbe.exec.command"}]},"code":409}
error: Apply failed with 4 conflicts: conflicts with "modified":
- .spec.template.spec.containers[name="probe"].readinessProbe.exec
- .spec.template.spec.containers[name="probe"].readinessProbe.exec.command
- .spec.template.spec.containers[name="probe"].readinessProbe.exec
- .spec.template.spec.containers[name="probe"].readinessProbe.exec.command
```

Note that the conflicts returned by the 409 error have duplicate fields, and completely omit at least 3 of the fields we are actually conflicting with.

### Anything else we need to know?

If we re-apply the original with `--force-conflicts`, then the correct data is applied, and the correct field managers are set, however if we do not want to force conflicts, the conflicting fields returned in the 409 error returned from the API server are incorrect.

I think the KEP is wrong.  A headless, selectorless Service: a) has no clusterIP (so IP family doesn't matter); and b) has user-defined endpoints (so we *can't* have an opinion about IP Family).  This case is handled specially in the registry code:

    if service.Spec.ClusterIP == api.ClusterIPNone {

        if len(service.Spec.Selector) == 0 {

            //                                                                                                                                              
            // At this stage we don't know what kind of endpoints (specifically
            // their IPFamilies) the user has assigned to this selectorless
            // service. We assume it has dual-stack and we default it to
            // RequireDualStack on any cluster (single- or dual-stack
            // configured).
            service.Spec.IPFamilyPolicy = &requireDualStack
            service.Spec.IPFamilies = []api.IPFamily{r.primaryIPFamily, otherFamily(r.primaryIPFamily)}
        } else {
```

body:
### What happened?

I have a daemonset with the rolling update strategy. I have `maxSurge` parameter set to a non zero value [which means](https://github.com/openshift/kubernetes/blob/cb4b47e5ddfbaf7844237b2e2eb2b0acfed5f1b5/pkg/apis/apps/validation/validation.go#L394-L402) that the `maxUnavailable` parameter is set to `0`. Hi, @alebedev87
Now I'm working for it and I have one question.

You expect that:
> The daemonset controller should just delete the old pods from the nodes which cannot be tolerated anymore.

However if master `Nodes` have taint as below(it's default setting of k8s), and `DaemonSet` which will be updated has no torelation, what do you expect to happen?
```yaml
 taints:
  - effect: NoSchedule
    key: node-role.kubernetes.io/master
```

I think the old `Pod` should remain without been updated and deleted according to the Taints and Tolerations mechanism.

For example:

`Before Update`
```
pod_on_master01_v1
pod_on_master02_v1
pod_on_master03_v1
pod_on_node01_v1
pod_on_node02_v1
pod_on_node03_v1
```

↓  Update DaemonSet

`After Update`
```
pod_on_master01_v1
pod_on_master02_v1
pod_on_master03_v1
pod_on_node01_v2
pod_on_node02_v2
pod_on_node03_v2
```

From the Taint section of Kubernetes document, 

- The `Node` having `NoSchedule` toleration means that no `Pod` will be able to schedule onto the `Node` unless the `Pod` has a matching toleration.(https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/taint-and-toleration/#concepts)
- The `Node` having `NoExecute` means that the `Pod` will be evicted from the `Node` unless the `Pod` has a matching toleration, and if the `Pod` has a matching toleration, it remains on the `Node`.(https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/taint-and-toleration/#taint-based-evictions)


So if master `Nodes` have taint as below, and `DaemonSet` which will be updated has no torelation, I think the old `Pod` should be deleted.
```yaml
 taints:
  - effect: NoExecute
    key: node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane
  - effect: NoSchedule
    key: node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane
```

For example:

`Before Update`
```
pod_on_master01_v1
pod_on_master02_v1
pod_on_master03_v1
pod_on_node01_v1
pod_on_node02_v1
pod_on_node03_v1
```

↓  Update DaemonSet

`After Update`
```
pod_on_node01_v2
pod_on_node02_v2
pod_on_node03_v2
```

What do you think about that?
I've created #119317 according to the above.

@mochizuki875: I think I'm fine with the approach to keep the old pods on the master nodes if the master nodes don't have the `NoExecute` taint.
The only doubt I have is about the status of the daemonset. I noticed that it changes according to the scheduling options, including the tolerations. You can see in the description that the number of the desired pods changes to 3 (only workers). So, according to your proposal we will see the difference in the status and the number of the really running pods (3 vs 6 if we take the example from the description).

Hi @alebedev87
> I think I'm fine with the approach to keep the old pods on the master nodes if the master nodes don't have the NoExecute taint.

Thanks for your consent.

> The only doubt I have is about the status of the `DaemonSet`. I noticed that it changes according to the scheduling options, including the tolerations. You can see in the description that the number of the desired pods changes to 3 (only workers). So, according to your proposal we will see the difference in the status and the number of the really running pods (3 vs 6 if we take the example from the description).

I've noticed that too.
In conclusion, I think the defference is no problem because:

- all nodes which don't match the schedule option should be excluded from target of `DaemonSet`
- daemon pods which is running excluded nodes should not be managed by `DaemonSet`


FYI: The implementation of updating `DaemonSet` status is as below.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/b2a9c06b2e7419691de5ea4f7d112baa2e00bc29/pkg/controller/daemon/daemon_controller.go#L1160-L1171

In this case, by updating `DaemonSet` without `tolerations`, 3 master with `taints` are no longer the target of `DaemonSet` and 3 daemon pods on them are no longer managed by `DaemonSet`.
3 daemon pods on master should depend on taints of master(`NoSchedule`: should remain , `NoExecute`:  should be deleted), and if we delete them, they should be deleted and not come back.

You can see `DaemonSet` status is that desired=3, current=3 even though there are actually 6 daemon pods running. 


So in this case, I think it is no problem that desired number of pods changes 6 to 3 and 6 daemon pods(3 pods on worker are managed by `DaemonSet`, the other are not) are running by updating without `tolerations`. 

You can see the similar case if you update `DaemonSet` by `OnDelete` updateStrategy.
- Create new `DaemonSet`
- It should be that:
  - desired: 6
  - running: 6
- Update `DaemonSet` by `OnDelete` updateStrategy without `tolerations`
- It should be that:
  - desired: 3
  - running: 6
- If you delete one pod on master, it will be deleted and not come back
  - desired: 3
  - running: 5

In my opinion we should remove the old pods that are running from the old revision when the NoSchedule tolerations or taints change. I think the rollout aspect and consistency of the DS takes precedence over the scheduling aspect. We are interested in running a new revision and not keeping old revisions running in currently unschedulable nodes. This applies to the `rollingUpdate` strategy that should automate transition between revisions and not bother users with manual removal of pods as compared to `onDelete` strategy.

Reproducibility/predicatability is also an issue, if you delete the updated DS and create the same DS you should achieve the same state of the cluster.

Please also take a look at https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/119317#pullrequestreview-1543685582

Thank your for your comment.

nodes.title: Exclude nodes from rolling update depending on tolerations
nodes.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

In this PR, exclude `Nodes` from daemon pod updating if the `tolerations` of it  dose not match the `taints` of `Nodes`.
It will cause update stuck if we try to rolling update `DaemonSet` which has non zero `maxSurge` and dose not have `tolerations` matching `Nodes` `taints`.
It's because all `Nodes` running `Pods` belonging to the previous `DaemonSet` are included in the update, regardless of the `tolerations` of the new `DaemonSet`.

#### Which issue(s) this PR fixes:

Fixes #118823

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
Revised the logic for DaemonSet rolling update to exclude nodes if scheduling constraints are not met.
This eliminates the problem of rolling updates to a DaemonSet getting stuck around tolerations.
```

title: Network policies only take effect when pods are assigned to the same node
body:
### What happened?

I configured it according to the network policy demonstrated in the official document, and found that sometimes it takes effect and sometimes it does not. After investigation, I finally found that this example only takes effect when busybox and nginx are assigned to the same node, and it does not take effect if they are not on the same node.

url: https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/declare-network-policy/

As shown in the figure, the first part is completely done according to the demonstration of the official document, just to keep the busybox container without '--rm', which can be seen through the command 'kubectl get pod, node -o wide', the first part busybox and nginx are always on the 'worker-130' node, and the expected result is correct. However, in the second part, I forcibly dispatched nginx to 'worker-131' and immediately lost the connection.

![image](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/assets/71317399/12d5c07a-ec8a-4f07-b20a-a8c096683d49)


### What did you expect to happen?

Network policies should not only take effect when the test container and the container under test are on the same node.

title: "Connection reset by peer" due to invalid conntrack packets
body:
### What happened?

When packets with sequence number out-of-window arrived k8s node, conntrack marked them as INVALID. kube-proxy will ignore them, without rewriting DNAT. However, there is no corresponding session link on the host, and the host sends a reset packet, causing the session link to be interrupted

### What did you expect to happen?

connection not reset

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/74839

### Anything else we need to know?

This problem can be solved by command：
iptables -t filter -I INPUT -p tcp -m conntrack --ctstate INVALID -j DROP

Similar issue:https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/74839
But this issue "drop" is placed on the forward chain, our scenario needs to be placed on the input chain.

/sig network

is this about pods with hostNetwork: true ?
if not, why is this a kube-proxy issue if the problem is in INPUT?
/assign @aojea
Yeah, to be clear - filter INPUT applies to packets which are going to be delivered to a process.  Is that kube-proxy's job to define?
The "How can we reproduce" sounds a bit like this _always_ happens. Here is a better instruction https://github.com/moby/libnetwork/issues/1090#issuecomment-747613353

IMO [this](https://github.com/moby/libnetwork/issues/1090#issuecomment-425421288) is the best description of the problem:
> The problem as already mentioned by @aaronlehmann is that benign "invalid" packets to the SNAT'ed container (caused for instance by TCP window overflow due to high throughput but slow client) are assigned to the host interface and considered incorrectly martians, which causes a connection reset.

> echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/netfilter/ip_conntrack_tcp_be_liberal

This may be a better solution than let `kube-proxy` add rules in the INPUT chain

hehe, ironically we should decide to `to_be_liberal` or  `to_be_strict`, one is a sysctl call the other is one (or two) iptables rules.

The iptables rule has also the side effect of breaking people (cc @cyclinder ) https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/94861#issuecomment-1545250481

If we switch to set the `sysctl` option, the change does not seem to be backportable.

> This may be a better solution than let kube-proxy add rules in the INPUT chain
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/117924#issuecomment-1545212625

I tend to agree with Lars, remove the iptables INVALID drop rule and set the sysctl, we are already setting more host sysctls 

@thockin @dcbw @danwinship what do you think? it will be nice to have some iptables hackers opinion too

I tried to recreate this problem on virtual en (kvm/qemu) by requsting a 100MB file with curl and do;
```
iptables -A INPUT -m statistic --mode random --probability 0.05 -j DROP
```
to provoke some packet loss. The transfer took longer time, but never failed.

IMO kube-proxy should not set any sysctls that are not literally _required_ for functionality that the user has explicitly opted into (eg `net.ipv4.ip_forward` for most network plugins). Kube-proxy does not own the host network namespace, and it should not be doing things that will affect _other people's_ host-network traffic, because if we do it's going to break some users. (See also: #94861.)

We can document that we think it's a good idea for users/distros to set `ip_conntrack_tcp_be_liberal`, and if we think it's almost always a better idea than not, we can warn at startup if it's not set, but (IMO) we shouldn't set it ourselves.

If we can get the same effect with an iptables rule that only affects kube-proxy's own traffic, then I think that's better than setting a sysctl that will also affect non-kube-proxy traffic.

If I understand the situation here correctly, if kube-proxy added a drop rule for the invalid conntrack packets, but then the administrator set `ip_conntrack_tcp_be_liberal`, then the result would be that conntrack would not mark some packets as invalid, and so our drop rule would just not get hit, and so our drop rule wouldn't interfere with the "better" sysctl-based solution?

> We can document that we think it's a good idea for users/distros to set ip_conntrack_tcp_be_liberal, and if we think it's almost always a better idea than not, we can warn at startup if it's not set, but (IMO) we shouldn't set it ourselves.

Agree in general.  We have done it in the past (e.g. route-localnet) and mostly it seems like a not-great idea.

> If we can get the same effect with an iptables rule that only affects kube-proxy's own traffic, then I think that's better than setting a sysctl that will also affect non-kube-proxy traffic.

Also agree.

If we see this as a known bug, please consider documenting it in https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/networking/virtual-ips/ - even if latest Kubernetes includes a fix (we can nevertheless point that out!)
I'll fix this in the next few days.

> We can document that we think it's a good idea for users/distros to set `ip_conntrack_tcp_be_liberal`, and if we think it's almost always a better idea than not, we can warn at startup if it's not set, but (IMO) we shouldn't set it ourselves.

From further googling, it seems like there have been situations in the past where people were setting that sysctl to work around bugs in conntrack, which were later fixed. I think this may be another such situation; it seems like our problem is that there is some state involving dropped or retransmitted packets which linux would cope with fine in the non-conntrack case, but which it doesn't handle in the conntrack case, unless "be_liberal" is set, and that seems like a bug.

Every time I look away from this set of issues/PRs for longer than 15 minutes I forget the exact scenario that causes the bug, but if someone could summarize it very clearly we could try dragging some kernel developers in.

(The regression test in the e2e suite creates a packet with an intentionally-bad sequence number, but it's not clear to me what sort of real-world issue that's supposed to be representing.)

> (The regression test in the e2e suite creates a packet with an intentionally-bad sequence number, but it's not clear to me what sort of real-world issue that's supposed to be representing.)

https://kubernetes.io/blog/2019/03/29/kube-proxy-subtleties-debugging-an-intermittent-connection-reset/

Thanks @aojea, now _that_ was an excellent article! Well written (_not_ TL;DR that is), and IMO perfect technical level. If there is some collection of recommended reading for persons who want to know about K8s networking, this article should be in it.

Hi  @aojea thank you for the [document](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2019/03/29/kube-proxy-subtleties-debugging-an-intermittent-connection-reset/) , it's really helpful!

I have some questions:

1. Per https://github.com/moby/libnetwork/issues/1090#issuecomment-488154993, should we update this sentence accordingly `ip_conntrack_tcp_be_liberal `==>` nf_conntrack_tcp_be_liberal`

> Make conntrack more liberal on packets, and don’t mark the packets as INVALID. In Linux, you can do this by echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/netfilter/ip_conntrack_tcp_be_liberal.

2. After we use the above workaround, would there any side effect for the cluster network or cluster nodes?

> > (The regression test in the e2e suite creates a packet with an intentionally-bad sequence number, but it's not clear to me what sort of real-world issue that's supposed to be representing.)
> 
> https://kubernetes.io/blog/2019/03/29/kube-proxy-subtleties-debugging-an-intermittent-connection-reset/

That says "this problem will occur if conntrack is unable to recognize a packet", but it doesn't explain the *real-world scenario* that causes conntrack to be unable to recognize a packet.

If we go to the kernel developers and say "manually injecting random incorrect packets into a conntrack'ed connection causes it to get confused", then they'll likely respond either "don't do that then" or "use `nf_conntrack_tcp_be_liberal`".

But if we can tell them something like "if a connection has a duplicated packet after a dropped packet, then conntrack gets confused", then that sounds a lot more like a bug in conntrack that they ought to fix, such that then everything will just work for everyone in the future without needing any DROP rules or sysctls.
So do we need to revert the drop rules? As @aojea mentioned in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/117924#issuecomment-1545651750 , it now seems that this makes sense.

There are three potential "fixes" here:
1. If this is unambiguously a conntrack bug, then we should figure out the details, and get the kernel devs to fix it. However, getting kernel bug fixes into all k8s clusters in the world takes "a long time", so even if it is a kernel bug, we should still think about the other fixes.
2. Individual cluster admins can use `nf_conntrack_tcp_be_liberal`. We should advertise this better, but we feel that it would be dubious to have kube-proxy set this flag itself (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/117924#issuecomment-1548163880).
3. As per https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/94861#issuecomment-1626025213 we could probably tweak the existing rule so that it didn't interfere with non-k8s packets ~and as suggested by the OP of this issue, we could add a similar rule to the INPUT chain (though this would need a bit of further thinking about to make sure we weren't introducing any new conflicts with non-k8s traffic)~.

We _could_ revert the DROP rules and tell people to use the sysctl instead (and actually, probably that's a better answer for _this_ issue than adding a new DROP rule to the INPUT chain is). But we'd need to warn users in advance if we were going to do that, since it would break existing clusters.

> and actually, probably that's a better answer for this issue than adding a new DROP rule to the INPUT chain is

Totally agree, This is a better fix for this issue. If this is a kernel bug and it gets fixed someday, we can easily tell the user that you don't need to set `nf_conntrack_tcp_be_liberal` anymore.

Also, If we revert the DROP rule, which can solve the routing asymmetry issue mentioned in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/94861, which is a big fix for us😄

> since it would break existing clusters.

Yes, We need to document it and tell the user. and In order not to break the existing cluster, Do we need a flag to decide if we need the DROP rule?  I'll make it default to `true`, and make it consistent with the current logic.

> Also, If we revert the DROP rule, which can solve the routing asymmetry issue mentioned in #94861, which is a big fix for us😄

but the change to only apply the DROP rule to pod traffic should also fix that

> Do we need a flag to decide if we need the DROP rule?

We should not require administrators to choose between "high-traffic TCP services work" and "asymmetric routing works". The current DROP rule is broken. We should either fix it to work with asymmetric routing, or else remove it and tell people who needed it to use the sysctl instead. In the latter case, we might want to make the transition via a feature gate. Then people who need asymmetric routing to work can enable the feature gate in Alpha (to make kube-proxy stop creating the DROP rule), and people who need high-traffic services to work but who didn't get the memo about using the sysctl can _disable_ the feature gate in Beta until they have a chance to update their node configs to set the right sysctl.

> but the change to only apply the DROP rule to pod traffic should also fix that

Refer to https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/94861#issuecomment-1545250481, The DROP rule to pod doesn't fix our case.  In our case, the pods of the external cluster subnet failed to access the pods of the cluster subnet to connect due to asymmetric routing, So the packet still matches The DROP rule to pod.
 
> In the latter case, we might want to make the transition via a feature gate

Do we need a KEP for this or only a feature gate?

In general, feature gates imply KEPs (and any change that will take multiple releases to complete, where we want to make sure we don't forget about it halfway through, should get a KEP, because we have processes for tracking those).

It doesn't have to be a _big_ KEP, and some of the sections of the KEP template will be irrelevant and can be omitted, because you're not introducing a new feature. (See https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/4005 for example.)

> In the latter case, we might want to make the transition via a feature gate. Then people who need asymmetric routing to work can enable the feature gate in Alpha (to make kube-proxy stop creating the DROP rule), and people who need high-traffic services to work but who didn't get the memo about using the sysctl can _disable_ the feature gate in Beta until they have a chance to update their node configs to set the right sysctl.

We are going to break users, unfortunatly features gates does not have the effect that we are assuming, and we know that  all the users have to set the "ip_conntrack_tcp_be_liberal" because eventually some connections will be broken.

I do no like to set sysctl, but 'm not in favor of replacing the rule and leaving the problem to users that may not even know what a sysctl is ...  agree the DROP rule is broken and breaks some esoteric but legit scenarios, but we are already setting sysctls, so I think that if we don't find any alternative to the DROP rule we should try to set the sysctl for the user by default
If we skip a KEP, make sure that the release team know to track the details (comms, docs, etc) as if it were a KEP. This is an important thing to track.
Should we at least triage this as Accepted?

/triage accepted

Some alternatives

1. remove DROP rule and ask users to set sysctl `ip_conntrack_tcp_be_liberal` (I'm not in favor per my previous comment and the least surprise principle)
2. remove DROP rule and we set sysctl `ip_conntrack_tcp_be_liberal` 
3. only set DROP rule if `ip_conntrack_tcp_be_liberal` is not set
4. control the DROP rule with a flag/config so users can opt-out if don't want to set it (they can decide to use the sysctl or live with that risk)
5. ...

I can accept KEP, but I think this may take multiple releases to complete. how about this?

- We remove the DROP rule
- Control the sysctl with a flag or a feature-gate.

If it's a flag, I believe it's relatively simple and we can finish it in 1.29. In the case of feature-gate, this may take multiple releases to complete.
If https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/120354 sets the `nf_conntrack_tcp_be_liberal` to true by default, we can safely remove the DROP rule

nodes.title: only drop invalid cstate packets if non liberal
nodes.body:
Conntrack invalid packets may cause unexpected and subtle bugs on esblished connections, because of that we install by default an iptables rules that drops the packets with this conntrack state.

However, there are network scenarios, specially those that use multihoming nodes, that may have legit traffic that is detected by conntrack as invalid, hence these iptables rules are causing problems dropping this traffic.

An alternative to solve the spurious problems caused by the invalid connectrack packets is to set the sysctl nf_conntrack_tcp_be_liberal option, but this is a system wide setting and we don't want kube-proxy to be opinionated about the whole node networking configuration.

Kube-proxy will only install the DROP rules for invalid conntrack states if the nf_conntrack_tcp_be_liberal is not set.


/kind bug
/kind cleanup
/kind feature

Fixes #117924, #94861

```release-note
Kube-proxy will only install the DROP rules for invalid conntrack states if the nf_conntrack_tcp_be_liberal is not set.
```

title: Service.Spec.LoadBalancerSourceRanges intent?
body:
### What happened?

/sig network

The documentation for Service.Spec.LoadBalancerSourceRanges copied from : https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/tree/master/pkg/apis/core#L3850
```
// Optional: If specified and supported by the platform, this will restrict traffic through the cloud-provider
// load-balancer will be restricted to the specified client IPs. This field will be ignored if the
// cloud-provider does not support the feature."
```

clearly states that this field is to be applied by cloud provider's on the network and/or the LB and/or cloud firewall. And specifically calls out the fact that this field is ignored if a cloud provider is not configured or does not support the field. The field itself subtly entails that `range` is an arbitrary `string` (not IP, we don't call that out) that is _meaningful_ to cloud provider but carries _no meaning_ to `kube-proxy` since it is not supposed to touch it

Yet `kube-proxy` seems to operate on this field and add corresponding iptables rules to the IPs in the field eg: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/proxy/iptables/proxier.go#L1270-L1278 

### What did you expect to happen?

We need a clear guidance for this field. because right now we are:
1. Duplicating the work of LB/cloud FW rules across both the cloud infra and the nodes.
2. Clouds operate using `tags`/`labels` to identify its own services' ip ranges, typically in cidr form. For example `Cloud XYZ` may use the `tag` `service ABC` to identify all the IP ranges used by service ABC on said cloud. Those ranges are can be in thousands cidrs which as you can tell will represent a massive problem if they go into iptables via the code above.
3. It creates a confusion about how this field relates to network security policies.


Possible solution around that is to create a new cli flag for kube-proxy (defaults to true) keeping the current behavior. When the flag is set to false then we stop creating these rules. Or revise the documentation for that flag and deal with the large # of cidrs ranges separatly. 




### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

I agree with you, I think that we should update the doc and, if the number of iptables rules created by this field is a concern, make it optional in kube-proxy ... the flag vs config is another topic in its own, last state is that kube-proxy use config and not flags :shrug:

(Which is wrong, sigh. API validation ensures that it is an array of CIDR strings, not an array of IPs.)

> Clouds operate using tags/labels to identify its own services' ip ranges, typically in cidr form. For example Cloud XYZ may use the tag service ABC to identify all the IP ranges used by service ABC on said cloud. Those ranges are can be in thousands cidrs which as you can tell will represent a massive problem if they go into iptables via the code above.

But how would they go into iptables? There is no way to refer to that cloud-specific set of IP ranges from a Kubernetes service

Thanks @danwinship I didn't know that they were validated (as cidrs or as IPs). Which means we need to update the docs anyway.

The point i am trying to make is, these shouldn't be applied on nodes. They are for the cloud provider to apply on LB or vnet's/VPC's firewall.

So, 2 points:
1. If you have GCP-style load balancers, the CloudProvider can choose to let kube-proxy handle LoadBalancerSourceRanges for it rather than implementing it itself. (I don't know if any actually do...)
2. With the current code, the LoadBalancerSourceRanges apply to pod-to-LB traffic as well, so we need to apply them in kube-proxy to take care of short-circuited traffic. Though if we didn't have to worry about point 1, then we could apply them only in the case where the LocalTrafficDetector indicates that the traffic is local. (And if we have a `--cluster-cidr` then we could just optimize out the actual rules if the entire cluster CIDR was either allowed or blocked.)

Do we know of any implementation that uses anything but CIDRs here?  They can't, right?  `GetLoadBalancerSourceRanges()` verifies they parse as CIDRs (weird place for that, but OK..).

I'll be first to admit this wasn't a great API - open-ended lists are bad.  But I think we can't realistically change it too much.  We could add a limit of 100 or 500 entries, but we can't even hard-fail, we can only return an API warning if you exceed that (because you know someone out there does).

Given that LBs can be "internal", we DO need to check short-cut traffic against them, as Dan said.

well, I think the answer is more "because none of this was rigorously designed, and that's the behavior we ended up with, and we can't change it now because of backward compatibility".
Agree with the idea that our degress of freedom are limited - close?

So do we expect alternative service proxy implementations to also "redundantly" implement this functionality?

(It appears that MetalLB expects that the proxy will do this for it.)

> So do we expect alternative service proxy implementations to also "redundantly" implement this functionality?

why redundant? I think that we can't assume LoadBalancer = Cloud Provider = Cloud Firewall ... MetalLB is a good example of why we can't assume that, so it will be only redundant for a subset of clusters

Funny thing is that the test we have to verify this field assumes that :upside_down_face: 

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/63dce95fd22109a60abdb440d7da327323065847/test/e2e/network/loadbalancer.go#L445-L447

well, the documentation of `LoadBalancerSourceRanges` explicitly states that it is the cloud provider that implements the feature, and that "`This field will be ignored if the cloud-provider does not support the feature.`"

> I think that we can't assume LoadBalancer = Cloud Provider

Maybe we _shouldn't_ assume that, but we absolutely assume that.

```
	// "LoadBalancer" builds on NodePort and creates an external load-balancer
	// (if supported in the current cloud)
```

> MetalLB is a good example of why we can't assume that

MetalLB is cheating and modifying Services behind Kubernetes's back in a way which is not documented as working/supported, and it only works as long as (a) you only use MetalLB in clusters with no cloud provider, and (b) you don't try to use any other component that also cheats in similar ways, since they would have no way to negotiate with each other, since they are doing unsupported things.

(Yes, we should absolutely make it possible to implement LoadBalancer services in a fully-supported way without being a CloudProvider, but we don't currently.)

In this regard, I think the cloud provider is "the person who assembled the cluster, including choosing metalLB".

So the question, I guess, is whether we should more strongly encourage other service implementations to do on-node source-range filtering when this API is used.  Given the intertwined nature of service IPs, LBIPs, and NAT, it seems like they have to, right?  

For example, if we didn't do this in kube-proxy and instead told cloud-providers to run their own agent for this, could they have done that?  By the time a packet hits the iptables `filter` table it has already been DNAT'ed, so we don't know which service was in play.

AIUI, MetalLB (at least in one mode) just uses BGP to redirect LB IP traffic to a particular node, and does not have any component that runs on the destination node itself. So they can't implement source ranges before the traffic hits the node (because there's no "load balancer host" that the traffic passes through that could do that), and they can't implement source ranges on the node itself (because they have no software running there). So if we say that they can't rely on kube-proxy to do it, they'd need to create/deploy a new component to run on the destination node to create the iptables rules themselves. Possible, but it definitely raises the question of "but why can't kube-proxy do it?".

> By the time a packet hits the iptables filter table it has already been DNAT'ed, so we don't know which service was in play

`iptables ... -m conntrack --ctstate DNAT --ctorigdst $LOADBALANCER_IP ...`

> iptables ... -m conntrack --ctstate DNAT --ctorigdst $LOADBALANCER_IP ...

> it definitely raises the question of "but why can't kube-proxy do it?".

Right. In a scenario where someone uses MetalLB to route to a node, and that node is running a non kube-proxy implementation of services, they might get no firewalling at all.  The API spec does say "This field will be ignored if the cloud-provider does not support the feature" so it's not technically WRONG.

First action: we should update the comments to say "This field might be ignored if the LB provider does not support...".

Second action: we don't really have an "implementors guide" for Services, and it would be weird to add "Implementations should strongly consider enforcing this" to the API guide.  Where would we document such a recommendation?

title: StatefulSet PodManagementPolicy Parallel affects updates
body:
<!-- Please use this template while reporting a bug and provide as much info as possible. Not doing so may result in your bug not being addressed in a timely manner. Thanks!

If the matter is security related, please disclose it privately via https://kubernetes.io/security/
-->


**What happened**:

Hi,

I'm trying to understand whether a behaviour we are observing in stateful sets with `Parallel` `PodManagementPolicy` is expected or if we are hitting a bug.

From the docs:

> Parallel pod management tells the StatefulSet controller to launch or terminate all Pods in parallel, and to not wait for Pods to become Running and Ready or completely terminated prior to launching or terminating another Pod. This option only affects the behavior for scaling operations. Updates are not affected.

I'm trying to understand the last bit "Updates are not affected". Unless I am misunderstanding the intention here, we expect that during scale up and down pods will be created and terminated in parallel. However, for the pods which will not be removed or added, I expected this to work similarly to `OrderedReady`.

The behaviour we are seeing does not match this expectation however.

Starting with this state:

```
NAME       READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
my-sts-0   0/1     Running   0          32m
my-sts-1   1/1     Running   0          32m
my-sts-2   1/1     Running   0          33m
```

Running a rolling update ignores the unready pod `0` and results in:

```
NAME       READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
my-sts-0   0/1     Running   0          32m
my-sts-1   1/1     Running   0          32m
my-sts-2   0/1     Terminating   0          33m
```
 
Is this the intended behaviour? If so, what do the docs mean by "Updates are not affected"?

**What you expected to happen**:

Since pod `0` is unready I would expect the StatefulSet update to not proceed until both pod `0` and `1` are ready.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:

* Create a StatefulSet with `Parallel` pod management policy.
* Get pod `0` to an unready state.
* Trigger a rolling update for the statefulset.

**Anything else we need to know?**:

Diving in the code I came across this line: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/792b4b1e32394a13c27741f71f14dd134d663a5f/pkg/controller/statefulset/stateful_set_control.go#L442

Which appears to be skipping waiting for pods to become ready for `Parallel` pod management policies regardless of whether the action which is about to take place is a scale up/down or an update.

**Environment**:
- Kubernetes version (use `kubectl version`):

```
Server Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"19+", GitVersion:"v1.19.3-dd1", GitCommit:"cca64583d7846303a3e9d3137e19e62a4be6bb58", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2020-10-15T07:50:03Z", GoVersion:"go1.15.2", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/amd64"}

Hey, In my opinion,  "Updates are not affected" applies when all replicas are fully ready and running before rolling update. In your case, my-sts-0 is not ready, which is approximately same as the case a statefulset is still in middle of parallel scaling, which will not prevent program from reaching  the point of rolling update  https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/792b4b1e32394a13c27741f71f14dd134d663a5f/pkg/controller/statefulset/stateful_set_control.go#L519 can be reached.

Hey 🙂 that code path can definitely be reached when the statefulset is in this state, but I think it should be prevented.

It's not quite the same as a parallel scale up even though it technically looks like one. For instance, it would be acceptable to add new pods while a pod is down, but terminating a second existing pod could violate disruption budgets and compromise quorums.

title: kube-proxy: Drop packets in INVALID state drops packets from outside the pod range
body:
**What happened**:
When kube-proxy is configured with a cluster-cidr range, it drops packets with an INVALID conntrack state for all sources on the KUBE-FORWARD chain. This is meant to prevent spurious retransmits in long-lived TCP connections to a service IP, but it prevents clusters from having asymmetrical routing on private subnets with services outside of a cluster. 

**What you expected to happen**:
Packets on the KUBE-FORWARD chain with an INVALID conntrack state should be dropped for only sources inside of the cluster-cidr if set.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:
N/A

**Anything else we need to know?**:
Change to drop INVALID conntrack packets was in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/74840. Backing out that commit and compiling is my current workaround.

**Environment**:
- Kubernetes version (use `kubectl version`): 1.17.2
- Cloud provider or hardware configuration:
- OS (e.g: `cat /etc/os-release`):
```

VERSION="7 (Core)"
ID="centos"
ID_LIKE="rhel fedora"
VERSION_ID="7"
PRETTY_NAME="CentOS Linux 7 (Core)"
ANSI_COLOR="0;31"

REDHAT_SUPPORT_PRODUCT="centos"
REDHAT_SUPPORT_PRODUCT_VERSION="7"
```
- Kernel (e.g. `uname -a`):
```Linux 3.10.0-1127.el7.x86_64 #1 SMP Tue Mar 31 23:36:51 UTC 2020 x86_64 x86_64 x86_64 GNU/Linux```

@thockin I can try to give a bit more context to our setup, but the knowledge I have around this all dates back to Feb, unfortuately, so I may have forgotten details.

We were replacing our mesos cluster with a kubernetes cluster in Feb and using a custom ingress solution (HAProxy w/an outside process configuring it for pod ips / mesos ip-ports) for both. The ingress nodes lived in the private subnet, but outside of the kubernetes cluster cidr range. When we upgraded from kubernetes 1.14 to kubernetes 1.15 (the first version with PR https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/74840) our ingress could no longer talk to any pod ips. I discovered that the KUBE-FORWARD chain had a rule to drop invalid packets, which was added in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/74840. Compiling kubernetes 1.15 without this commit fixed our problems, and we have been carrying that patch forward ever since. I would like to get rid of our forked kubernetes, hence this ticket.

When I was writing this ticket up, I also found [a blog post](https://www.growse.com/2020/01/23/adventures-with-asymmetric-routing-and-firewalls.html) also mentions the same issue with the iptables dropping INVALID conntrack state packets near the end, regarding asymmetrical routing.

>Edit, OK I get the original problem, but still don't understand why packets from outside the pod range would not exhibit #74839, thereby requiring yet another revisit of this problem.

I think you are correct, I can imagine packets from outside of a cluster could exhibit the same behavior as packets inside the cluster and cause spurious resets. However, I  am wondering if kube-proxy should be managing packets from outside of the cluster on a node... That seems outside of the scope of kube-proxy.

```
nf_conntrack_tcp_be_liberal - BOOLEAN
	0 - disabled (default)
	not 0 - enabled

	Be conservative in what you do, be liberal in what you accept from others.
	If it's non-zero, we mark only out of window RST segments as INVALID.
```

@aojea I don't understand how that will help me here. The packets with a ctstate INVALID are not generated due to conntrack saturation ([as described here](https://technology.lastminute.com/chasing-k8s-connection-reset-issue/)), but due to asymmetric routing in our network. See [the blog post I linked earlier](https://www.growse.com/2020/01/23/adventures-with-asymmetric-routing-and-firewalls.html) for an example of a similar setup.

We were bit by this too after revisiting an old service that had been unused since the heady days of pre-#74840, and would also like to see the proposed patch merged (or a configuration option to prevent insertion of the INVALID state drop rule - either suits us).

I unfortunately don't have any useful input as to setting up for reproduction. In our case we have a pretty odd anycast set up with a small pool of (public) addresses managed by calico. 

However I do seem to have a dirty workaround for small clusters. By setting notrack (ctstate UNTRACKED?) in the raw table for packets in our specific ranges that would otherwise match ctstate INVALID, the packets aren't dropped. Which may be of help to someone else who finds this issue.

We are seeing something very similar on large file downloads and our issue exactly fits this one's subject.
These RESET (corrected after @aojea) are happening intermittently and I am seeing similar behavior mentioned in the blog mentioned below. I am unsure if someone has found a workaround for this issue or not, so yeah my +1 to this issue being looked up by the community.

> @aojea I don't understand how that will help me here. The packets with a ctstate INVALID are not generated due to conntrack saturation ([as described here](https://technology.lastminute.com/chasing-k8s-connection-reset-issue/)), but due to asymmetric routing in our network. See [the blog post I linked earlier](https://www.growse.com/2020/01/23/adventures-with-asymmetric-routing-and-firewalls.html) for an example of a similar setup.
@abhiTamrakar We're using https://github.com/kakao/network-node-manager as a solution for the connection reset we were seeing and might fix this issue.

Let me try to avoid that this thread derails and see if I can get current status:

> These REJECTs are happening intermittently and I am seeing similar behavior mentioned in the blog mentioned below.

1. kube-proxy install rules to drop INVALID cstate connections, this solves the ~REJECT~ RESET problems
2. there are some scenarios, with asymmetric routing per example, that this rules may drop unrelated traffic.

The request is to remove the rule that drops those INVALID states or to try to restrict it, and that can cause that people start to have the  ~REJECT~ RESET problems and drops again.

If we have a reproducer we can be more precise in the final solution, but removing one rule without any strong evidence in kube-proxy is very risky

As a workaround for the asymetric routing problem, I suggested to set the nf_conntrack_tcp_be_liberal on the kernel:
```
sysctl -w net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_tcp_be_liberal=1
```
I think that will solve the problems, it will be good if someone can test it and provide feedback

> Let me try to avoid that this thread derails and see if I can get current status:

No sadly, its my bad, it is not REJECT, it is RESET that's happening and conntrack has nothing to do with it, mostly (I hope). Kubeproxy is doing what is intended but specifically when there are external agents in play, the packet doesn't sends an ACK back to the response of SYN-ACK.
Our case, we hit A to initiate a download, A calls B to get the action completed to generate download data for the user finally via their browser.
A and B both are on k8s, we saw A starts and a complete cycle goes for sometime until there multiple parallel downloads requested where few gets completed and few gets a RESET.
On primary debugging, it appears that RESET was getting invoked by the pod but pod is just sending a RST-ACK not RST itself.
The missing packet is never found in the default route, unless we see that there is a chance where ACK is missed and we found some lines in tcpdump with missing sequence for ACKs. Thats why i doubt my issue is related here.

One more weird coincidence is few downloads have spurious transmission.

Thankyou, I will take a look, but mostly I would like to wait before using it, debug more to understand the actual cause and then act on it.

sorry , I wanted to say RESET, thanks for catching it.
If you think is different and you can provide information and how to reproduce it, I suggest you to open a new issue

I will sure do, when it is different. For now I would like to watch and submit my findings if it is related.
PS: sysctl -w net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_tcp_be_liberal=1 is already implemented and we are testing if it does something helpful. so far it doesn't looks like it. thanks for your help.

title: kmsv2: consider removing KMS from /livez checks
body:
<!-- Please use this template while reporting a bug and provide as much info as possible. Not doing so may result in your bug not being addressed in a timely manner. Thanks!

If the matter is security related, please disclose it privately via https://kubernetes.io/security/
-->


**What happened**:
kube-apiserver goes unhealthy and restarts when a kms provider returns PermissionDenied on Encrypt/Decrypt requests. This may happen when the permission to encrypt and decrypt gets revoked.

**What you expected to happen**:
I expected kube-apiserver to stay healthy and return errors on types covered by the kms provider.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:
Revoke permission to encrypt/decrypt data by a KMS key.

**Anything else we need to know?**:
[Code](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ed4c2dbf9211bec3e080488b0fd67a9725759a45/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/options/encryptionconfig/config.go#L139) just does classic `err != nil` so I think that checking error code here will resolve the issue.

nodes.body: /sig api-machinery
Is an API server which does not have the permission required to successfully read and write secrets healthy?
/assign @immutableT
/cc @logicalhan
@cheftako says he believes there is a workaround, disabling the KMS check in the manifest file.

I think that it is the desired behavior for kube-apiserver to return !OK when it is unable to encrypt/decrypt secrets.
However, restarting kube-apiserver due to the failure of the livenessProbe (as pointed out by @cheftako) would not help. Hence, excluding kms-providers from the liveness check makes sense.

> Is an API server which does not have the permission required to successfully read and write secrets healthy?

This is of course open to interpretation but it seems that since API server works with many objects, not necessarily requiring secrets, it should be considered healthy, no?

> I think that it is the desired behavior for kube-apiserver to return !OK when it is unable to encrypt/decrypt secrets.
However, restarting kube-apiserver due to the failure of the livenessProbe (as pointed out by @cheftako) would not help. Hence, excluding kms-providers from the liveness check makes sense.

There is a (not merged) pull request that addresses /livez not being OK because of failures of KMS providers' health checks:     https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/83588. I'm really looking forward to getting the code merged, but I'm not sure whether it is possible to "take over" the pull request. Or should I just create a new one?

I agree with @MAnyKey it would be better to merge #83588 to avoid these type of issues in the future.
@liggitt @cheftako WDYT?

> This is of course open to interpretation but it seems that since API server works with many objects, not necessarily requiring secrets, it should be considered healthy, no?

I think successful access to the configured storage is relevant to server health. Allowing KMS health to be excluded from healthz/livez if desired by the API server operator is fine, but defaulting the API server to reporting healthy when it cannot read/write secrets (including secrets that need to be read internally as part of service account token authentication) seems like a harmful default to me.

> > This is of course open to interpretation but it seems that since API server works with many objects, not necessarily requiring secrets, it should be considered healthy, no?
> 
> I think successful access to the configured storage is relevant to server health. Allowing KMS health to be excluded from healthz/livez if desired by the API server operator is fine, but defaulting the API server to reporting healthy when it cannot read/write secrets (including secrets that need to be read internally as part of service account token authentication) seems like a harmful default to me.

I hate (and am not actually trying) to bring up the dreaded component-status, but I think we may be conflating concepts/mechanism here. To me healthz/livez is a signal to the kubelet that something is wrong. Specifically it indicates a failure which may be fixed by the kubelet restarting the process/container (https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-liveness-readiness-startup-probes/#define-a-liveness-command). I do not believe that the KMS failures will in any way be helped by restarting the api-server/container. It seems like we need an alternate signal that the system is unhealthy (intended for some higher level entity than the kubelet).

I agree with what people are saying above, which I is summarized by the following statement:

`KMS health is not appropriate as a liveness check.`

However, I personally do believe that KMS health checks may be appropriate as a readiness check.
I also suspect that that is what @liggitt and @cheftako are saying.

title: kubectl drain error message confusing when using with operator
body:
/kind bug

**What happened**:
Scenario:
- You run an etcd cluster with etcd-operator
- You drain a node with etcd-operator on it.

You get a message like:
```
$ kubectl drain $NODE
pods not managed by ReplicationController, ReplicaSet, Job, DaemonSet or StatefulSet (use --force to override): example-etcd-cluster-0002
```
This error message is not useful, given that Operators are popular and recommended.

**What you expected to happen**:
No error message.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:
```
# PREREQ: have a Cluster.  

# Install coreos operator as follows:
mkdir coreos
cd coreos
git clone https://github.com/coreos/etcd-operator
cd etcd-operator/
example/rbac/create_role.sh
kubectl create -f example/deployment.yaml
kubectl get customresourcedefinitions

# Make an etcd cluster
kubectl create -f example/example-etcd-cluster.yaml
kubectl get pods -L etcd_cluster -l etcd_cluster=example-etcd-cluster
kubectl get etcdcluster example-etcd-cluster -o json | jq .status.members
# Wait until some guys are ready
watch "kubectl get etcdcluster example-etcd-cluster -o json | jq .status.members"

# Find a node that has an etcd pod on it. Call it $NODE.
# in example, NODE="gke-cluster-2-default-pool-4904abf8-mt8t"
$ kubectl drain $NODE
node "gke-cluster-2-default-pool-4904abf8-mt8t" already cordoned
error: pods with local storage (use --delete-local-data to override): example-etcd-cluster-0004; pods not managed by ReplicationController, ReplicaSet, Job, DaemonSet or StatefulSet (use --force to override): example-etcd-cluster-0004, fun2, kube-proxy-gke-cluster-2-default-pool-4904abf8-mt8t; DaemonSet-managed pods (use --ignore-daemonsets to ignore): fluentd-gcp-v2.0.9-bc4jm
```
The offending message is **pods not managed by ReplicationController, ReplicaSet, Job, DaemonSet or StatefulSet (use --force to override)**.

**Anything else we need to know?**:

**Environment**:
- Kubernetes version (use `kubectl version`): `
Client Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"7", GitVersion:"v1.7.0", GitCommit:"d3ada0119e776222f11ec7945e6d860061339aad", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2017-06-30T09:51:01Z", GoVersion:"go1.8.3", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"darwin/amd64"}
Server Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"7+", GitVersion:"v1.7.8-gke.0", GitCommit:"a7061d4b09b53ab4099e3b5ca3e80fb172e1b018", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2017-10-10T18:48:45Z", GoVersion:"go1.8.3", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/amd64"}
`

nodes.body: This is making cluster automation extremely painful, is there any good work-around other than manually terminating/rescheduling the pods to new nodes when this happens?
This appears to be fixed in kubectl 1.10 and beyond.

For anyone who encounters this same problem, a potential workaround is to just delete the node that it's having a problem draining, then running the rolling-update again.  IE:

`failed to drain node "node-name": error draining node: Unknown controller kind "bad-controller"`
`$ kubectl delete node "node-name"`

This worked for my situation, at least.
Manually deleting the blocking pods from already cordoned off nodes helps as a workaround. After that draining should be possible.
